passages.title: Revelation sent down for pure devotion
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Sūrat az-Zumar opens by naming where the Qur'an came from — and then draws the one conclusion that follows from that origin: worship belongs to Allah alone, purely, with nothing mixed into it. Ayah 1 establishes the *source* of the Book. Ayah 2 establishes its *truth* and issues the command that flows from it. Ayah 3 states the principle in absolute terms and then confronts the single argument by which people have always tried to escape it. Read together, these three ayat are one continuous movement: **a revelation this pure, from a source this exalted, can only be answered with a devotion equally pure.**

Ibn Kathir titles his comment on this opening simply: *The Order for Tawhid and the Refutation of Shirk.*

**A note before we begin.** An-Nasa'i recorded from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "used to fast until we would say, 'He does not want to break fast,' and he would not fast until we would say, 'He does not want to fast.' And he ﷺ used to recite Banī Isrā'īl [al-Isrā'] and az-Zumar every night." This sūrah was part of the Prophet's ﷺ nightly companionship with the Qur'an. That is worth carrying with you as you read it.

---

## Ayah 1: where the Book comes from

The sūrah does not begin with a command or a warning. It begins with a statement of origin: **تَنزِيلُ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ مِنَ ٱللَّهِ** — *The revelation of this Book is from Allah.*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us that the revelation of this Book — "which is the magnificent Qur'an" — is *from Him*, and that it is "truth in which there is no doubt whatsoever." The Book did not arise from below and work its way up. It came down.

Ibn Kathir then places two other ayat alongside it to let them illuminate each other. The first traces the route of the descent: *"And truly, this is a revelation from the Lord of the creatures, which the trustworthy Rūḥ (Jibrīl) has brought down upon your heart that you may be one of the warners, in the plain Arabic language"* (26:192–195). The second describes what such an origin guarantees: *"And verily, it is a mighty Book. Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it — sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise"* (41:41–42).

**The two names.** The sender is identified by two of His names, and neither is decorative.

- **al-'Azīz** — Ibn Kathir glosses it as "the Almighty, All-Powerful." This is might that cannot be resisted or overruled. A Book from *al-'Azīz* cannot be suppressed by those who oppose it, and its commands cannot be safely ignored.
- **al-Ḥakīm** — "the All-Wise," and Ibn Kathir specifies the scope: wise **"in all that He says, does, legislates and decrees."** Not merely wise in the abstract, but wise in every word revealed, every act done, every law given, every destiny apportioned.

Put the two together and you have the answer to two different objections before they are raised. Power without wisdom would be mere force; wisdom without power would be good advice you could safely decline. From *al-'Azīz al-Ḥakīm*, the Book is both unassailable and unimprovable.

---

## Ayah 2: sent down in truth — therefore worship Him purely

Ayah 1 spoke of the Book in the third person: *the revelation of this Book is from Allah*. Ayah 2 shifts to direct speech — **إِنَّآ أَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ بِٱلْحَقِّ** — *Verily, We have sent down the Book to you in truth.* The Prophet ﷺ is now addressed personally. And the very next words are the command that follows from it: *"So, worship Allah by doing religious deeds sincerely for Him only."*

Notice the order of the sentence. First the statement — the Book is from Allah, and it came down in truth. Then, on that basis, the command — worship, and worship stripped of every partner.

Ibn Kathir unfolds the command in three motions: "so worship Allah Alone with no partner or associate, **and call mankind to that**, and teach them that it is not right to worship anyone or anything except Him Alone, and He has no partner, equal or rival." The command is not only inward. The one who has received the Book purifies his own worship and then carries that purity outward to others.

**What "dīn" means here.** The word *dīn* is often translated "religion," which can make the ayah sound narrower than it is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise: *dīn* in this place "means worship, submission, devotion or obedience which is inclusive of adhering to all religious injunctions." So the command is not merely that your ritual acts be sincere. It is that your entire posture of obedience — everything you do because Allah said so — be directed to Him and to no one else.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the structure of the two statements. In ayah 2 the address is to the Prophet ﷺ himself, commanded "to make the worship of and obedience to Allah sincere and exclusive for Him, so as there remains no trace of shirk or of any hypocrisy or false pretension." Then ayah 3 comes as reinforcement — "to emphasize the first statement in that sincerity in worship is the exclusive right of Allah and no one else, other than Him deserves it." First the command, then the principle that grounds it.

---

## Ayah 3, first half: the standard of acceptance

**أَلَا لِلَّهِ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْخَالِصُ** — *Surely, the religion is for Allah only;* or, as another rendering has it, *Indeed, sincere devotion is due only to Allah.*

Ibn Kathir draws the consequence with no softening: *"He will not accept any deed unless it is done purely and sincerely for Him Alone, with no partner or associate."*

This is the hinge of the whole passage. It is not merely that shirk is a sin among sins. It is that a share given to another **disqualifies the act itself.** The measure is not how much of the deed was for Allah; the measure is whether anything else was allowed in at all.

---

## Ayah 3, second half: the argument the messengers came to demolish

Now the ayah quotes the objection, in the idolaters' own voice: *"We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah."*

**They were not atheists.** This is the detail that makes the passage land. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the Mushriks of Arabia — "even the common people among them during that period of time" — "more or less had the same belief that Allah Ta'ālā is the creator, owner and master in all matters." They did not deny Allah. They wanted access to Him.

**How the reasoning worked.** According to Ibn Kathir, what motivated their worship was that "they made their idols in the image of the angels — or so they claim — and when they worship those images it is like worshipping the angels, so that they will intercede with Allah for them to help and give them provision and other worldly needs." As for the resurrection, "they denied it and did not believe in it" — which tells you what they were actually after: this world, not the next.

Qatādah, as-Suddī, and Mālik — narrating from Zayd bin Aslam and Ibn Zayd — explained *"only that they may bring us near to Allah"* as meaning: "So that they may intercede for us and bring us closer to Him." They were not seeking to replace Allah. They were seeking a shortcut to Him.

**Where the picture came from.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the origin and the mental model behind it precisely. It was when "the Shaitan instigated them" that "they started making idols in the image of angels, as they imagined they would be." From there they "compared Allah's nearness with that of the worldly kings where a courtier who is pleased with someone could put in a good word for him with the king and have him included among his inner circle. So, they surmised that the angels too could recommend anyone they chose very much like the royal courtiers of their world." They knew perfectly well, Maʿārif notes, that "these idols made by them had no consciousness, reason or power" — the idol was never the point; the imagined patronage behind it was. Maʿārif's verdict is blunt: "all these ideas they nursed were totally false, in fact, they were nothing but satanic deception."

**How far it reached.** Ibn Kathir records that during the Jāhiliyyah, when they performed Ḥajj, their *talbiyah* ran: **"At Your service, You have no partner** *except the partner You have; he and all that he owns belong to You."*

That line is worth reading twice, and the observation that follows is our own rather than Ibn Kathir's: they could not even declare Allah's oneness without inserting an exception into it. The corruption was not placed alongside the affirmation; it was slipped inside it.

**Not a stray error — the error.** Ibn Kathir writes that "this pretentious argument which the idolators of all times, ancient and modern, used as evidence is what the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all, came to refute and forbid, and to call people to worship Allah Alone with no partner or associate. This is something that the idolators themselves invented; Allah did not give them permission for it, nor does He approve of it; indeed, He hates it and forbids it." He cites: *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger proclaiming: Worship Allah, and avoid Ṭāghūt"* (16:36), and *"And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me"* (21:25).

---

## Why the argument collapses

The sources dismantle it from several directions at once.

**1. The angels are servants, not courtiers.** Ibn Kathir: "the angels in the heavens, those who are close to Him and others, are all servants who submit humbly to Allah. They do not intercede with Him except by His leave for the one with whom He is pleased. **They are not like the princes and ministers of their kings** who intercede with them without their permission for both those whom the kings like and those whom they hate." The entire analogy is imported from human politics and does not survive contact with reality. Hence: *"So put not forward similitudes for Allah"* (16:74) — and Ibn Kathir adds, "Exalted be Allah far above that."

**2. Intercession is by permission only.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that angels "cannot intercede on behalf of anyone before Allah on their own, unless they are allowed to make their intercession about a particular person," and cites: *"And how many angels there are in the heavens whose intercession cannot benefit anyone at all, but after Allah allows it for whomsoever He wills and pleases"* (53:26). Intercession is real, but it is not leverage. It is granted downward by Allah; it is never obtained upward by cultivating the intercessor.

**3. The angels themselves would recoil.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises two further objections: who could even say "whether or not these idols happen to be on the real form of the angels"? And even if they were, "one cannot expect angels close to Allah showing their pleasure over being worshipped by somebody on the earth. In fact, they temperamentally hate everything that Allah Ta'ālā does not like." The nearer a creature is to Allah, the more it detests being made a rival to Him.

**4. The angels will say so on the Day of Judgement.** Ibn Kathir cites the scene: *"And remember the Day when He will gather them all together, then He will say to the angels: 'Was it you that these people used to worship?' They will say: 'Glorified be You! You are our Walī instead of them. Nay, but they used to worship the Jinn; most of them were believers in them'"* (34:40–41). The imagined patrons disown their clients in public.

---

## "Allah will judge between them"

The ayah closes with two statements that settle the matter.

*"Verily, Allah will judge between them concerning that wherein they differ."* Ibn Kathir: this means on the Day of Resurrection — "He will judge between His creation on the Day of Resurrection and will reward or punish each person according to his deeds." The dispute over who deserves worship is not left unresolved. It is adjourned, not dropped.

*"Truly, Allah guides not him who is a liar, and a disbeliever."* Ibn Kathir explains: "He will not show true guidance to one who deliberately tells lies about Allah and whose heart rejects the signs and proof of Allah." Two things are named together there: a lie told about Allah, and a heart that has already turned down the evidence. Guidance is withheld not arbitrarily, but from someone who has made his decision about the truth before it reached him.

---

## Living it: what pure devotion asks of you

It would be comfortable to file all this under "ancient idolatry." The sources do not permit that.

**The mixed intention.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, citing Qurtubi, that it was reported from Sayyidnā Abū Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that someone said before the Holy Prophet ﷺ: *"Yā Rasūlallāh, there are occasions when I give in charity or do a favor to somebody, but my intention gets mixed up — I do look forward to seek the pleasure of Allah thereby, but I also hope that people will praise me for it."* The Prophet ﷺ answered: *"By the One in whose hands lies the life of Muhammad, Allah Ta'ālā does not like anything in which someone or something else has been associated as a partner or sharer with Him."* Then he recited this very ayah as proof: **"Remember, Allah alone deserves the exclusive submission."**

That exchange brings ayah 3 out of history and into the ordinary Muslim's chest. The man was not worshipping an idol. He was giving charity — with a second audience in mind. And the ayah was recited *to him*.

**Deeds are weighed, not counted.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops this into a principle: several ayat of the Qur'an show that deeds are not measured with Allah by number but by weight — *"and We shall place scales to do justice on the Day of Judgment"* (21:47). Read together with our passage, Maʿārif concludes, "the value and weight of deeds is judged by the amount of sincerity with which they are performed." A ledger of many acts thinly meant can weigh less than one act wholly meant.

**What complete sincerity involves.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here, and this is worth reading slowly. Perfect sincerity "cannot be achieved without perfect faith, because perfect sincerity means that one should not take someone as having intrinsic power to benefit or harm someone other than Allah, nor take someone other than Allah as disposer of one's acts, nor allow the thought of someone other than Allah enter into any act of worship or obedience **of his volition**."

And then the mercy that keeps this from crushing anyone: **"As for non-voluntary scruples, Allah Ta'ālā forgives them."** The passing thought that arrives uninvited during ṣalāh is not what is being condemned. What is condemned is the share you *choose* to give away.

**Why the Companions' deeds weighed so much.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion: the noble Ṣaḥābah "are the front line of Muslims. Their practice of prayers and good deeds may not appear to be very prominent numerically. But, despite all this, the reason why the single insignificant most of their deeds was superior to the highest of the high deeds of the rest of the Ummah was no other but their very perfection of *īmān* (faith) and perfection of *ikhlās* (sincerity)."

**A closing observation from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.** Commenting on this passage, it remarks that in one respect the polytheists of that era stood above the materialist disbelief of our own, which "already deny the very existence of Allah Ta'ālā." Its verdict on a world that has multiplied comfort while losing peace is memorable: "Ever-new gadgets of comfort proliferate, but real comfort remains missing. Advancements in health care have never been at a level they are today, but there is a matching abundance of diseases hitherto unheard of. Security arrangements, police, guards, surveillance abound, but the graph of crime keeps rising." It ends with a Persian quip that fits this whole passage: **"In the middle of the house, I forgot the master of the house!"**

---

## Holding the three together

Ayah 1 tells you Who sent the Book and that He is unassailable in power and flawless in wisdom. Ayah 2 tells you it came down in truth, and therefore — *therefore* — worship Him with the dīn made purely His. Ayah 3 tells you that this purity is not an optional excellence but the very condition of acceptance, and then removes the last excuse: the idea that you might route your devotion through anyone at all in the hope of getting closer.

There is no intermediary in the design. The Book came down from Him. The worship goes back to Him. Nothing is meant to stand in between.

passages.title: Allah takes no son; signs in creation
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers one of the oldest lies told about Allah — that He has taken offspring — and then, instead of merely arguing, it walks the listener out under the sky and back into his mother's womb to show him who Allah actually is. Ayah 4 refutes the claim on its own terms; ayat 5 and 6 make the refutation unnecessary by parading the evidence of Allah's sole creatorship across the heavens, the night and day, the herds, and the reader's own body. The thread holding all three together is the surah's opening command: worship Allah with religion made sincerely His alone.

**A note on the surah itself.** An-Nasa'i recorded that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to fast until they would say he did not want to break his fast, and would not fast until they would say he did not want to fast — "and he ﷺ used to recite Bani Isra'il [Al-Isra'] and Az-Zumar every night." A surah he ﷺ returned to nightly is worth reading slowly.

## Where ayah 4 comes from

Ibn Kathir sets the scene from the surah's first three ayat. Allah declares the Qur'an to be sent down from Him — *al-'Aziz* (the Almighty, meaning, Ibn Kathir says, "the Almighty, All-Powerful") and *al-Ḥakīm* (the All-Wise, "in all that He says, does, legislates and decrees") — and then commands the Prophet ﷺ to worship Allah alone, sincerely, and to call people to that. "Surely, the religion is for Allah only" means, Ibn Kathir says, that **He will not accept any deed unless it is done purely and sincerely for Him alone, with no partner or associate.**

Against this comes the idolaters' famous excuse: *"We worship them only that they may bring us near to Allah."* Ibn Kathir explains what actually motivated them — they had made their idols in the image of the angels, or so they claimed, so that worshipping the images was like worshipping the angels, who would then intercede with Allah for their provision and worldly needs. As for the resurrection, they denied it outright. Qatadah, As-Suddi, and Malik narrating from Zayd bin Aslam and Ibn Zayd all read the phrase the same way: "So that they may intercede for us and bring us closer to Him."

That self-contradiction was audible in their own worship. In the days of *Jahiliyyah* — the age of ignorance before Islam — their *talbiyah*, the call they recited aloud when performing Hajj, ran: "At Your service, You have no partner **except the partner You have**; he and all that he owns belong to You." They confessed His sole ownership in one breath and installed a partner in the next.

Ibn Kathir calls this "the pretentious argument which the idolators of all times, ancient and modern, used as evidence," and says the Messengers came precisely to refute and forbid it, and to call people to worship Allah alone. This, he adds, was something the idolaters invented for themselves: Allah never permitted it, does not approve of it, and indeed hates and forbids it.

He also corrects the picture underneath it. The angels are not courtiers. They "are all servants who submit humbly to Allah. They do not intercede with Him except by His leave for the one with whom He is pleased" — unlike the princes and ministers of a human king, who intercede without permission, for people the king likes and people he hates alike. Hence: *"So put not forward similitudes for Allah"* (16:74).

From that same false picture comes the claim ayah 4 answers. Ibn Kathir names the parties: the ignorant idolaters claimed the angels were Allah's offspring, and, he writes, the stubborn Jews and Christians made that claim of 'Uzayr and 'Isa.

## Ayah 4: an "if" designed to be impossible

*"Had Allah willed to take a son, He could have chosen whom He willed out of those whom He created. But glory be to Him! He is Allah, the One, the Irresistible."*

**This is not a concession.** Ibn Kathir is emphatic: the matter is not as they claim, and "this is a conditional sentence which does not imply that this happened or that it is permitted; indeed, it is impossible. The aim is only to point out the ignorance of their claims." He places it alongside two sister ayat built the same way — *"Had We intended to take a pastime, We could surely have taken it from Us"* (21:17), and *"Say: If the Most Gracious had a son, then I am the first of worshippers"* (43:81) — and states the principle plainly: "it is permissible to form a conditional sentence referring to something that is impossible if it serves the purposes of the speaker."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows why the supposition dismantles itself.** It treats the ayah as a refutation of those who said the angels were Allah's progeny, taken up as "a supposition of the impossible." Children are not imposed on anyone — certainly not on Allah — so if He had offspring it could only be by His intention and will. Grant that supposition for a moment. Everything other than Him is something He created, so He "would have picked up one of them to be His progeny." And this is exactly what the ayah says: He could have chosen from among those He created.

That is where the argument closes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: children "have to be of the same genus as the father, and the created cannot be of the same genus as the creator, therefore, the intention to have progeny from the created becomes impossible." A chosen creature remains a creature. Whatever you elevate — an angel, a righteous man — you have only promoted a servant, and a promoted servant is still not a son. The claim collapses without ever needing to be attacked from outside.

**Then the ayah turns from argument to glorification:** *Subhānahu — huwa Allāhu 'l-Wāhidu 'l-Qahhār.* Ibn Kathir: exalted and sanctified be He above the idea that He could have any offspring, "for He is the One, the Only, the Unique, the Self-Sufficient Master to Whom everything is enslaved and is in need of. He is the One Who is independent of all else, Who has subjugated all things and they submit humbly to Him. Blessed and exalted be He far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say."

Notice the pairing of the two names. *Al-Wāhid*, the One, the Only, the Unique — as Ibn Kathir glosses it — leaves no room for a second alongside Him. *Al-Qahhār*, rendered here as the Irresistible, is explained by Ibn Kathir as the One who has subjugated all things so that they submit humbly to Him. A being to whom everything is enslaved and in need stands in no relation of kinship to any of it.

## Ayah 5: the evidence overhead

Having denied the false claim, the passage now simply shows you Allah at work. Ibn Kathir titles this section *Evidence of the Power and Oneness of Allah*: Allah tells us that He is the Creator of what is in the heavens and on earth and what is between them, "the Sovereign and Controller alternating the night and day."

**"He created the heavens and the earth with truth"** — or, as the passage is rendered here, *for a purpose*.

**"He wraps the night over the day and He wraps the day over the night."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word *takwīr*: it "means to throw something on top of the other and thereby hide it." It adds that the Qur'an has deliberately described the alternation of night and day in terms of common perception — when night comes, it is as if a curtain has been thrown against the light of the day, and when the day comes, the darkness of the night goes behind the curtain. Anyone in any century can verify that image from a rooftop.

Ibn Kathir reads it as ceaseless motion: "He has subjugated them and He causes them to alternate without ceasing, each seeking the other rapidly," citing *"He brings the night as a cover over the day, seeking it rapidly"* (7:54). This, he notes, is the meaning narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, Mujahid, Qatadah, As-Suddi, and others.

**"And He has subjected the sun and the moon. Each running for an appointed term."** They are not powers in their own right; they have been made to serve. Ibn Kathir: the appointed term means "a period of time that is known to Allah, then it will come to an end on the Day of Resurrection." The sun you plan your day by has a fixed last day.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on a question modern readers bring to the text. The phrase *"each one of them moving for an appointed term"* tells us that both the sun and the moon move, and believing what the Qur'an states is obligatory. But it adds an important discipline: "Scientific researches in astronomy and geology are not the subject of the noble Qur'an, or of any other scripture... Scientific findings, old or new, keep changing all the time. Qur'anic facts are changeless." As for whether sunrise and sunset relate to the movement of the earth or to the movement of these bodies themselves, the Qur'an "neither confirms nor rejects it. Hence, there is no hitch in accepting what experience or experiment bears out." A believer neither forces the Qur'an to be a science textbook nor feels threatened when the textbooks are revised.

**"Verily, He is the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving."** Ibn Kathir on this pairing: "beside His might, greatness and pride, He is Oft-Forgiving to those who disobey Him but then turn to Him in repentance." The ayah has just described a Lord who wraps night over day and drives the sun on a fixed term — and it ends by telling the person who has been worshipping someone else that the door back is open.

## Ayah 6: the evidence inside you

The lens now turns from the cosmos to the human being, and finally to the darkness in which he was assembled.

**"He created you from a single person; then made from him his wife."** Ibn Kathir: He created you — "with all your varied races, types, languages and colors" — from a single soul, who was Adam, peace be upon him; and his wife, Hawwa', peace be upon her, was made from him. He cites the parallel opening of Surat An-Nisa': *"O mankind! Have Taqwa of your Lord, Who created you from a single person, and from him He created his wife, and from them both He created many men and women"* (4:1). Every difference the human race quarrels over traces back to one origin.

**"And He has sent down for you of cattle eight pairs."** Ibn Kathir identifies them as the eight kinds listed in Surat Al-An'am: a pair of sheep, a pair of goats, a pair of camels, and a pair of oxen. But why "sent down" for animals that walk the earth? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, explains that a major factor in their creation is the water sent down from the sky — so it can be said that they too were, as it were, sent down. The Qur'an speaks the same way of clothing, *"We have sent down to you clothing"* (7:26), and of iron, *"and We sent down iron"* (57:25). The purpose in each case "is to emphasize that these things were created through the intrinsic power of Allah Ta'ala, and that they were given to human beings as His blessings." What you buy at the market came down to you.

**"He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three veils of darkness."** Ibn Kathir traces the stages by their Arabic names: everyone of you is originally a *nutfah*, then he becomes an *'alaqah*, then he becomes a *mudghah* — three successive stages of formation — then "he is created and becomes flesh and bones and nerves and veins, and the *Ruh* (soul) is breathed into him, and he becomes another type of creation." Hence *"So Blessed is Allah, the Best of creators"* (23:14).

As for the three veils of darkness: the darkness of the womb, the darkness of the placenta which blankets and protects the child, and the darkness of the belly. Ibn Kathir reports this as the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Abu Malik, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, As-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks *why* it was done this way, and gives two reasons. **First, the gradualness is wisdom toward the mother.** It was well within Allah's power to have the infant come to be created whole and complete in a single instant; but "such was the dictate of wisdom and expedient consideration that it was not done." A process of gradualness was chosen instead — "creation after creation" — so that the woman in whose womb this "mini universe" was taking shape "should gradually become used to bearing its burden." **Second, the hiddenness itself is part of the wonder.** This marvel of beauty and efficiency, "provided with hundreds of precision gadgets, hair-thin veins to carry life-blood and spiritual input," was not made to look like the products of common industrialists in spacious factories under glowing lights. It "reached its completion at a place shielded by three layers of darkness" — a location so hidden that, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, it beats all imagination.

## The question the passage ends on

*"Such is Allah your Lord. His is the kingdom. La ilaha illa Huwa. How then are you turned away?"*

Ibn Kathir gathers it: "the One Who created the heavens and the earth and everything in between, and created you and your forefathers, is the Lord. To Him belong sovereignty and control over all of that." *Lā ilāha illā Huwa* means "no one else should be worshipped except Him alone with no partner or associate." And the closing *fa-annā tusrafūn* he renders as a rebuke you are meant to feel: "how can you worship anything besides Him? What has happened to your minds?"

That is the architecture of the passage. Ayah 4 shows that the son-claim cannot even be coherently supposed. Ayat 5 and 6 show a Lord who alternates night and day, subjects sun and moon to a fixed term, brought all humanity out of one soul, sent down the herds you live off, and shaped you personally in three layers of darkness. After that, turning to anyone else is not merely sinful; it is unintelligible.

## Living it

**Guard the sincerity.** The idolaters' logic — an intermediary to carry me closer — is, as Ibn Kathir says, the argument of idolaters "ancient and modern." The corrective is the surah's own opening: Allah will not accept any deed unless it is done purely and sincerely for Him alone.

**Use the evidence you already have.** This passage does not send you to a library. Watch the light go; notice the sun keeping an appointment it did not set; remember that you were formed in the dark without ever being consulted. Ayah 6 is arguing with your own body as its witness.

**And do not despair of returning.** The ayah that establishes His might names Him, in the same breath, the Oft-Forgiving — Oft-Forgiving, Ibn Kathir says, "to those who disobey Him but then turn to Him in repentance."

passages.title: Are they equal? The ingrate and the devout
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat hold up two lives side by side and ask you to look honestly at which one is yours. The thread running through them is this: Allah gains nothing from your faith and loses nothing by your rejection — so everything at stake here is *yours*. The passage lays down that principle, paints the ungrateful man, paints the worshipper who stands in the night, asks the unanswerable question "Are those who know equal to those who know not?", and then turns from portraits to instruction and speaks directly to the believers.

## "Allah is not in need of you"

The passage opens by removing a misunderstanding people carry without noticing it — the quiet assumption that our worship somehow adds to Allah, that He needs us on His side.

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is here telling us He is Independent and **has no need of anything in creation**. He connects it to the words of Musa, peace be upon him, to his people: "If you disbelieve, you and all on earth together, then verily, Allah is Rich, Owner of all praise" (14:8). Notice the scale of that: not one man's disbelief, not one nation's — every single human being on earth, together, and the balance of Allah's majesty does not move by a hair.

Ibn Kathir then cites what is recorded **in Sahih Muslim**, where Allah says:

> "O My servants, if the first and the last of you, men and Jinn alike, were all to be as evil as the most evil man among you, that would not diminish from My sovereignty in the least."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point in one plain line: neither does your faith bring any benefit to Allah, nor does your disbelief or ingratitude cause Him any loss.

This is not coldness. It is the removal of a bargaining chip. When you grasp that Allah needs nothing from you, obedience stops being a favour you do Him and becomes what it actually is — a mercy He is offering you.

## What Allah loves, and what He merely wills

Straight after that comes a sentence of extraordinary tenderness: **"He likes not disbelief for His servants."** Ibn Kathir glosses it: He does not like it, and He does not enjoin it. And its counterpart — "And if you are grateful, He is pleased therewith for you" — means He likes this for you *and He will increase His favour upon you*.

Read that carefully. Allah does not merely tolerate your gratitude; He is *pleased* by it, and answers it with more.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key word. **Riḍāʾ** (رِضاء) means love, liking, pleasure, or to intend to do something without objection. Its opposite, **sakhaṭ** (سَخَط), means to detest something or to take it to be objectionable — and, crucially, a thing can be found objectionable *even while* it is coupled with intention.

That last nuance is what lets Maʿārif ul Qurʼān settle an old question here.

**The point of creed.** Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah believe that nothing good or bad, faith or disbelief, can come into existence without the will and intention of Allah; for anything at all to exist, His intention is a binding condition. But His *pleasure and favour* relate only to faith and good deeds. Disbelief, shirk (the ascribing of partners to Allah) and acts of disobedience are things He does not like. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes what Shaykh al-Islām Nawawī writes in his book *al-Uṣūl wa-l-Ḍawābiṭ*, and gives this translation of it (citing *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*):

> The creed (madhhab) of people who follow the truth (ahl-ul-haqq) is to believe in destiny (al-qadr) and that all existents, good or bad, come into existence under the decision (qada') and destination (qadar) of Allah Ta'ala, and Allah Ta'ala does make the intention to create these, but He dislikes acts of disobedience and sin - though, the intention of creating these materializes in view of some wise consideration which He alone knows in His most exalted majesty.

So there is no contradiction between "everything happens by Allah's will" and "Allah does not like disbelief." Willing that a thing exist and being pleased with that thing are two different matters, and the ayah keeps them distinct.

## No one carries your load

The ayah then closes every escape route. "No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another." Ibn Kathir: no person can bear anything for another; **each person will be asked about his own affairs**. No ancestor's merit, no leader's authority, no crowd to hide inside.

Then: "Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you what you used to do. Verily, He is the All-Knower of that which is in breasts." Ibn Kathir's comment is one short sentence — **nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him**. The reckoning is not only of what you did; it reaches the chest, to the motive nobody else ever saw.

## The portrait of the ingrate

Now the Qur'an stops arguing and starts describing, and the description is uncomfortably familiar.

"And when some hurt touches man, he cries to his Lord, **turning to Him in repentance**." Ibn Kathir: at times of need, he prays to Allah and seeks His help alone, not associating anything with Him. Adversity strips a person's theology down to the truth that was always underneath. He becomes, for a moment, a pure monotheist.

Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat alongside it. The one about the sea: "And when harm touches you upon the sea, those that you call upon vanish from you except Him. But when He brings you safe to land, you turn away. And man is ever ungrateful" (17:67). And: "And when harm touches man, he invokes Us, lying on his side, or sitting or standing. But when We have removed his harm from him, he passes on as if he had never invoked Us for a harm that touched him!" (10:12).

"But when He bestows a favor upon him from Himself, he forgets that for which he cried for before." Ibn Kathir: at the time of ease, he forgets that supplication and prayer. The rescue itself becomes the anaesthetic.

And it does not stop at forgetting. "And he sets up rivals to Allah, **in order to mislead others from His path**." Ibn Kathir: at times of ease, he associates others in worship with Allah and sets up rivals to Him. The man who was rescued by turning to Allah alone now spends his restored strength pulling other people away from that.

**The verdict.** "Say: 'Take pleasure in your disbelief for a while, surely, you are (one) of the dwellers of the Fire!'" Ibn Kathir explains that this is said to those whose way this is, and that it is **a stern threat and solemn warning** — a command in form, a sentence in substance. He places two ayat beside it: "Say: 'Enjoy! But certainly, your destination is the Fire!'" (14:30), and "We let them enjoy for a little while, then in the end We shall oblige them to (enter) a great torment" (31:24). That little word — *for a while*, *for a little while* — is where the whole weight sits. Everything the ingrate has is real; it is just very short.

## The one who stands through the hours of the night

Here the passage turns, and the turn is built into the grammar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the opening word **ammán** (أَمَّنْ) is a combination of two words: *am*, an interrogative particle, and *man*, a relative pronoun ("the one who"). Scholars of exegesis say a sentence has been left unspoken before it — an ellipsis the listener is meant to supply. The full sense is that the disbeliever, having just been told to go and enjoy the fruits of his disbelief, is asked: *are you better, or is it the obedient believer who is mentioned next?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the question: "Can (such people be equal to) the one who worships during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing, fearing the Hereafter and having hopes in his Lord's mercy?" The Qur'an does not bother to spell the comparison out; it simply lets the second portrait stand next to the first, and lets you feel the answer.

**Qānit — what kind of obedience?** Ibn Kathir explains "Is one who is obedient to Allah, Ana'a Al-Layl prostrating and standing" as meaning one who is humble and fears Allah when he prostrates and stands in prayer, and reports from Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him): "The obedient one is one who obeys Allah and His Messenger ﷺ." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the word *qānit* has been explained variously, and that the explanation which comprehends all those meanings is the one from Ibn Masʿūd — **devotedly obedient**.

And when *qānit* is used in connection with ṣalāh — as in "Stand before Allah in total devotion" (2:238) — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurṭubī, gives it a very concrete shape: the person who lowers his gaze in ṣalāh, does not look right and left, does not play with his body or his clothes, and does not voluntarily let his mind turn to anything of his worldly life. And it adds a mercy: any incidence of forgetfulness, or an involuntary intrusive thought, would not be considered contrary to this. Devotion is measured by what you turn toward, not by thoughts that arrive uninvited.

**Ānāʾ al-layl — the hours of the night.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd that this means **in the depths of the night**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the expression denotes the early, the middle and the last part of the night, and notes (citing Qurṭubī) that some early commentators identified the time between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ as also included in it — which puts this within reach of an ordinary working life, not only of the specialist in night prayer.

By the same route, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates that Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said that a person who wishes Allah to make the reckoning on the plains of Resurrection easy on him should so manage himself that Allah finds him in the state of **sujūd** (prostration) and **qiyām** (standing) during the darkness of the night, in a condition in which he is concerned about his fate in the Hereafter yet is hoping for the mercy of Allah.

**Fear and hope together.** That inner state is exactly what the ayah names: "fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord." Ibn Kathir says this means that in his worship he feels both fear and hope; both are essential in worship, and **fear should be stronger during one's lifetime**, while **at the time of death, hope is uppermost**.

For this he cites what Imām ʿAbd bin Ḥumayd recorded in his *Musnad* from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon a man who was dying, and said to him, 'How do you feel?' He said, 'I am both afraid and hopeful.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "These do not co-exist in a person's heart at times such as this, but Allah will give him what he hopes for and protect him from that which he fears."

Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by At-Tirmidhī, An-Nasāʾī in *Al-Yawm wal-Laylah*, and Ibn Mājah, from the hadith of Yasār bin Ḥātim from Jaʿfar bin Sulaymān, and that At-Tirmidhī said, "Gharīb" — a term from the technical vocabulary the hadith scholars use in grading reports.

Ibn Kathir also records that Imām Aḥmad reported from Tamīm Ad-Dārī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Whoever recites one hundred Ayat in one night, it will be recorded as if he prayed all night."

This, Ibn Kathir adds, was also recorded by An-Nasāʾī in *Al-Yawm wal-Laylah*. A hundred ayat is a reachable thing — and it is offered here as a door into exactly the night-worship the ayah has just described.

**"Are those who know equal to those who know not?"** Ibn Kathir reads the question as continuous with everything before it: is *this* one — the one who stands and prostrates in the night, in fear and hope — equal to the one who sets up rivals to Allah to mislead men from His path? They are not equal before Allah. And the closing line, "It is only men of understanding who will remember," means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that the only one who will understand the difference between them is the one who has understanding. The knowledge in question is not information you can hold at arm's length; it is the kind that changes what you do with your nights.

## "O My servants who believe"

The passage ends by turning to the believers with a direct address — and note the honour in it: *My servants*.

**Taqwā first.** Ibn Kathir: Allah commands His believing servants to remain steadfast in their obedience and to have taqwā of Him — taqwā being the watchful consciousness of Allah that makes a servant guard himself and keep within His commands.

**"Good is for those who do good in this world."** Ibn Kathir explains: the one who does good deeds in this world will have a good reward **in this world and in the Hereafter** — the return begins before you die.

**"And Allah's earth is spacious."** Mujāhid's comment, cited by Ibn Kathir, is stripped of all softness: *"So emigrate through it and strive hard and keep away from idols."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why this sentence sits exactly here. Good deeds have just been enjoined; a person might come up with the excuse, "the city or country I live in, or the social milieu around me, stops me from doing good deeds." The sentence carries the answer: if adherence to Allah's injunctions is genuinely difficult while living in some particular country, city or social setup, then leave it — Allah's earth is wide enough; go and live in a place and a surrounding that helps you remain obedient. This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, persuades a person to migrate from a place in which he cannot dutifully follow and observe what his religion enjoins.

**"Only those who are patient shall receive their reward in full, without reckoning."** This is the passage's final and largest promise. Ibn Kathir cites al-Awzāʿī: their reward will not be weighed or measured; they will be given an immense reward. And as-Suddī, briefly: "In Paradise."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings of *bi-ghayri ḥisāb* (without measure). First: the reward of those who endure ordeals will not be given under any pre-determined calculation or measure; it comes without calculation or reckoning, in a spirit of generosity at its most sublime. Second: some have interpreted the expression in the sense of request or claim — in this worldly life, if something is due to you from someone, you have to initiate the claim for it; but with Allah, those who observe patience are given their reward without any request or claim.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then relates that Qatādah reports from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day of Judgement a Scale of Justice will be set in place; when the people who gave charity come forward, whatever they gave will be weighed and they will be given their full reward against it, and likewise acts of worship such as ṣalāh and ḥajj will be weighed and their reward duly given. But when those come who stood patient against trials and tribulations, for them there will be no measure and no weight — their reward will be rolled down towards them without calculation, measure or reckoning, because Allah has said, "Certainly those who observe patience will be given their reward in full without measure." So much so that people who lived their worldly lives in perfect peace and comfort would wish that their bodies had been shredded with scissors in the world, so that they too might have earned such a return for endurance.

**What is this ṣabr?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that Imām Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) took *al-ṣābirūn* here to mean people who endure hardships and remain patient over the sorrows of this mortal life. Some elders have said it means people who hold their self in check against acts of disobedience and sin. Qurṭubī observes that when the word *ṣābir* is uttered unaccompanied by another word, it invariably means the person who is patient against the hardship of making his desiring self abstain from sins; and when it is used of someone remaining patient against a particular distress, it is coupled with other words naming that distress ("patient against such and such"). Both meanings are honoured; the unqualified word leans toward the harder, quieter patience — the daily refusal of what your soul wants. And Allah knows best.

## Living it

The passage gives you a very small number of concrete things to carry away.

- **Stop imagining you are doing Allah a favour.** He is not in need of you. Your worship is a mercy extended to you, not a service rendered to Him.
- **Watch what you do after the rescue.** The whole indictment in this passage is not about the prayer in the storm — that part everybody gets right. It is about the forgetting afterwards. The test of that midnight duʿāʾ is what you are like three months after it is answered.
- **Take some of the night.** Even a hundred ayat; even the hours between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ. Ibn ʿAbbās tied an easy reckoning on the plains of Resurrection to being found prostrating and standing in the darkness.
- **Keep both wings.** Fear the Hereafter and hope in His mercy — fear stronger while you have life left to correct, hope uppermost at the end.
- **Change your surroundings if they are defeating you.** Allah's earth is wide. Go and live where the surroundings help you obey.
- **And when you are simply enduring** — a hardship you cannot fix, or the long refusal of a sin you badly want — know that this is the one account that is not weighed, because there is no measure large enough.

passages.title: Say: I am commanded to worship sincerely
passages.tafsir:
Six ayat in which Allah puts words into the mouth of His Messenger ﷺ. The command **قُلۡ**, *Qul*, "Say," comes four times across these ayat, and each time what follows is a personal declaration in the first person: *I* am commanded, *I* am afraid, *I* worship. The thread running through all six is one claim stated from every angle: worship belongs to Allah alone and must be offered with undivided sincerity — and the alternative is a loss that Ibn Kathir's rendering calls "a manifest loss."

## The setting: ayah 10, and why it matters here

These ayat land on the back of ayah 10, and Ibn Kathir treats 10–12 as one movement under a single heading: **"The Command for Taqwa, Emigration and to worship Him alone with all Sincerity."** There Allah tells the Prophet ﷺ to say: *"O My servants who believe, have Taqwa of your Lord. Good is for those who do good in this world, and Allah's earth is spacious! Only those who are patient shall receive their reward in full, without reckoning."*

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that Allah commands His believing servants to remain steadfast in their obedience and to have Taqwa of Him. He explains "good is for those who do good in this world" to mean that the one who does good deeds in this world will have a good reward in this world *and* in the Hereafter. On "and Allah's earth is spacious," he quotes the early commentator **Mujahid**: "So emigrate through it and strive hard and keep away from idols."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why that sentence sits exactly there. Good deeds have just been enjoined — and this might prompt someone to come up with the excuse that the city or country he lives in, or the social setting he is stuck in, stops him from doing good deeds. The words "and the earth of Allah is wide" carry the answer to that excuse: if you find adherence to Allah's injunctions difficult while living in some particular country, city or social setup, then leave it; the earth of Allah is wide enough. Go and live at a place, and in a surrounding, that is conducive to remaining obedient to the Divine commandments. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this persuades one to migrate — *hijrah* — from a place in which one cannot dutifully follow and observe what his religion has enjoined.

That is the doorway into ayah 11. A man told to worship Allah with total sincerity in a hostile setting will feel the cost of it. He is being told: the cost is real, but so is the option of moving, and so is the reward.

**"Without reckoning."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on *bi-ghayri ḥisāb*. It means the reward of those who endure ordeals will not be given to them under some pre-determined calculations or measures; it will be sans-calculation, sans-reckoning, in a spirit of generosity at its most sublime. Some others have interpreted the expression in the sense of *request* or *claim*: in this worldly life, if something is due to you from someone, you have to initiate the claim for it — but with Allah, those who observe patience will be given their reward without any request or claim. Ibn Kathir cites **Al-'Awza'i** to a similar effect: "Their reward will not be weighed or measured; they will be given an immense reward." **As-Suddi** said it means "In Paradise."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates here — Qatadah reporting from Sayyidna Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) — that the Prophet ﷺ said: on the Day of Judgment a Scale of Justice will be set in place. When people who had given Sadaqah come forward, whatever they gave will be weighed and they will be given their full reward against it. Acts of worship such as Salah and Hajj will likewise be weighed and their reward duly given. But when those who stood patient against trials and tribulations come, for them there will be no measure and no weight at all; their return and reward will be rolled down towards them without calculation, measure or reckoning — because Allah has said, *"Certainly those who observe patience will be given their reward in full without measure."* So much so that people who had lived their worldly life in perfect peace and comfort would wish that their bodies had been shredded with scissors during that life, so that they too might have earned a similar return for their endurance. *(The source relates this narration without naming a collection, so it is conveyed here only as the source gives it.)*

**Who are "the patient"?** The commentators differed, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the difference rather than settling it. **Imam Malik** took *aṣ-ṣābirūn* here to mean people who endure hardships and remain patient over the sorrows of the mortal life. Some elders said it means people who hold their self in check against acts of disobedience and sin. **Qurtubi** offers a linguistic observation that leans towards the second: when the word *ṣābir* ("patient") is uttered unaccompanied by some other word, it invariably means a person who observes patience against the hardships involved in making one's desiring self abstain from sins; and when the word is used of a person who remains patient against a distress, it is coupled with other words — *ṣābir ʿalā kadhā*, "one who is patient against such and such distress." And Allah knows best.

## Ayah 11: the command that shaped a life

> *Say: "Verily, I am commanded to worship Allah, making religion sincerely for Him."*

Notice the form of it. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to say "I have chosen this" or "this is my view." He is told to say **"I am commanded."** He stands under the same authority he is calling others to. What he asks of them, he does not exempt himself from.

Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and exact: *"I am commanded to worship Allah alone in all sincerity, with no partner or associate."* Two things are named in one phrase — Allah alone as the object of worship, and sincerity as the manner of it. Neither is enough by itself. Worship aimed at the right One with a divided heart, and worship offered wholeheartedly to the wrong one, are both failures. This is *ikhlāṣ*: worship kept purely for Allah, with no partner and no associate mixed into it.

## Ayah 12: "the first of the Muslims"

> *And I am commanded (this) in order that I may be the first of the Muslims.*

Ibn Kathir quotes this ayah as the close of the same movement he began at ayah 10, under his heading about Taqwa, emigration, and worshipping Him alone with all sincerity — and he adds no commentary to it. So the plain wording is left to stand as it is: the same Messenger ﷺ who has just been told to say "I am commanded to worship Allah, making religion sincerely for Him" is told in the same breath that he is commanded to be the first of the Muslims — those who submit.

## Ayah 13: the Messenger himself is afraid

> *Say: "Verily, if I disobey my Lord, I am afraid of the torment of a great Day."*

Ibn Kathir is arresting here. He introduces it: Allah says, say **"O Muhammad, even though you are the Messenger of Allah."** The "great Day," he explains, means the Day of Resurrection.

And then the point that turns the ayah on the reader: this is **a conditional sentence** — an "if." It is not a report that the Prophet ﷺ disobeyed; it is a statement of what disobedience would deserve, framed as a supposition. And, Ibn Kathir says, if what is referred to here applies to the Prophet ﷺ, **it applies even more so to others.**

Sit with that. The most beloved of Allah's creation is instructed to voice fear of that Day under such a condition. There is no rank that puts a person beyond the reach of Allah's justice, and no station of closeness that makes fear of Him unnecessary. Anyone who imagines his own piety, lineage, service or knowledge has bought him exemption is claiming what the Messenger ﷺ himself was not given to claim.

## Ayah 14–15: the same words again — and then a turn

> *Say: "Allah Alone I worship by doing religious deeds sincerely for His sake only. So, worship what you like besides Him."*

Ayah 14 restates ayah 11, but no longer as a report of what he was ordered to do — now as what he actually does. Ibn Kathir renders it *"Allah Alone I worship by doing religious deeds sincerely for His sake only."* The same two elements return: Allah alone, and sincerity in the deeds offered to Him.

Then comes the sentence that can be misread: *"So, worship what you like besides Him."* This is not permission. Ibn Kathir says plainly that it is **"a threat, and a disowning of them."** It is the tone of one who has finished arguing: go ahead, then — take whatever you want as your god, and see where it leaves you. It is the disavowal of a man who will not blur the line between his worship and theirs.

And the seeing-where-it-leaves-you follows at once:

> *Say: "The losers are those who will lose themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Verily, that will be a manifest loss!"*

Ibn Kathir explains "the losers" as meaning **the greatest losers of all**. And what is lost here is not property but **themselves** — the one asset a person cannot re-earn — and their families with them.

His explanation of losing one's family is one of the most sobering lines in the passage: it means **they will be separated and will never meet again** — whether their families have gone to Paradise and they have gone to Hell, or all of them have gone to Hell, they will never meet or feel happiness again. Even shared ruin brings no company. And of "a manifest loss" Ibn Kathir says: this is **the clearest and most obvious loss**. Every other loss a person fears in this life is partial and temporary; this one takes the self, the people, and the future in a single stroke.

## Ayah 16: fire above and fire below — and what it is for

> *They shall have coverings of Fire, above them and covering (of Fire) beneath them. With this Allah frightens His servants: "O My servants, therefore have Taqwa of Me!"*

The word is **ظُلَل** (*ẓulal*) — rendered in the sources as "layers" and as "coverings." The picture is of being enclosed: something over them and something under them, with nowhere in between that is not fire. Ibn Kathir sets two other ayat beside it to fix the image:

- *"Theirs will be a bed of Hell (Fire), and over them coverings (of Hell-fire). Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers"* (7:41)
- *"On the Day when the torment (Hell-fire) shall cover them from above them and from underneath their feet, and it will be said: 'Taste what you used to do.'"* (29:55)

A covering, by nature, is what a person takes shelter under. Here what should shade him is itself the punishment, and the ground beneath him has become the same.

Then the ayah does something remarkable: it tells you why you were just told this. **ذَٰلِكَ يُخَوِّفُ اللَّهُ بِهِ عِبَادَهُ** — *"With this Allah frightens His servants."* Ibn Kathir explains: Allah tells us about this, **which will undoubtedly come to pass, to frighten His servants, so that they will keep away from unlawful things and from sin.**

That reframes the whole description. It is not told to crush anyone. It is a warning issued in time, to people still able to act on it, so that they turn away from what would take them there. The fear itself is a mercy, because it is being given to you now rather than shown to you then.

And the closing words: **يَا عِبَادِ فَاتَّقُونِ** — *"O My servants, therefore have Taqwa of Me!"* Ibn Kathir: it means *"fear My wrath, My anger, My punishment and My vengeance."*

**Notice the frame.** The passage opened at ayah 10 with *"O My servants who believe, have Taqwa of your Lord"* and closes at ayah 16 with *"O My servants, therefore have Taqwa of Me."* The same address, the same command, at both ends — and everything in between (sincerity, patience, migration, fear, loss, fire) sits inside that frame. Notice too whom the warning is for: Ibn Kathir says it is told to frighten **His servants**, so that they keep away from the unlawful and from sin. The people being warned are the people still being addressed as His own.

## Living it

- **Purify the *what for*, not only the *what*.** Ayah 11 and ayah 14 both attach *mukhliṣan* — sincerity — to worship already being performed. As Ibn Kathir puts it, worship of Allah alone, in all sincerity, with no partner or associate. The question is not only whether you prayed, gave, or fasted, but whether anything besides Allah was mixed into it.
- **Do not let closeness to Allah breed security from Him.** If the Prophet ﷺ was told to voice fear of that Day under a condition, then, in Ibn Kathir's words, it applies even more so to others.
- **Take your surroundings seriously.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading of "the earth of Allah is wide" refuses the excuse that one's city or social setting makes obedience impossible — and Mujahid's words tie emigration to striving hard and to keeping away from idols. Where a setting genuinely prevents you from observing what your religion enjoins, the Qur'an points to the door rather than to resignation.
- **Value patience at Allah's rate, not yours.** The reward of those who endure is not given under pre-determined calculations or measures; it comes without reckoning — and, on one reading reported by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, without your even having to ask for it.
- **Hear the warning as it was meant.** Ibn Kathir says the description of the Fire is given to frighten His servants so that they will keep away from unlawful things and from sin. Its purpose is that you act now, while acting is still possible.

passages.title: Good news for those who shun false gods
passages.tafsir:
This passage draws a portrait of the people Allah calls "My servants" — those who refused false worship, listened to what was said, and chose the best of it — and then sets them against the person for whom the sentence of punishment has already fallen due. The four ayat move in one arc: **who these people are (17), how their minds work (18), who they are *not* (19), and where they end up (20)** — from a heart that turned away from idols to rooms built one above another in Paradise.

## Ayah 17: shunning the false gods, turning to Allah

The verse does not say "those who avoid At-Taghut" and leave it there. It specifies: *avoid At-Taghut by not worshipping them*. (*Taghut* is what the passage's translation renders as "false gods" — the false objects to which worship is wrongly directed.) Ibn Kathir takes the phrase exactly this way — the avoidance being praised is the avoidance of *worship* directed to false objects. What is being commended is not a vague distaste for idolatry but a refusal to bend the neck to anything besides Allah. And the sentence has a second half that completes it: they **turned to Allah**. Ibn Kathir describes them as those "who avoided worshipping idols and turned to the worship of Ar-Rahman." Shunning falsehood is only half a life; the other half is where you take your worship instead.

**Who was this revealed about?** Ibn Kathir reports from 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, narrating from his father, that this was revealed concerning **Zayd bin 'Amr bin Nufayl, Abu Dharr, and Salman Al-Farisi**, may Allah be pleased with them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions the same three, citing Qurtubi, and fills in why each fits: Zayd Ibn 'Amr Ibn Nufayl "used to hate shirk and idol worship even during the days of Jahiliyyah" — that is, before Islam came. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari and Salman al-Farisi listened to people of different religions — the mushriks, the Jews, the Christians — and saw their ways of life, and it was only then that they embraced Islam, finding the teachings of the Qur'an to be the best and preferring them.

Ibn Kathir is careful here, and his caution is worth learning from. He says: **"The correct view is that it includes them and all others"** who avoided worshipping idols and turned to the worship of Ar-Rahman. An occasion of revelation names the first people the verse landed on; it does not fence the verse in around them. The door these three walked through stays open. "These are the people," Ibn Kathir says, "for whom there is good news in this world and in the Hereafter."

**"So announce the good news to My servants."** Notice the shift: Allah has just described them in the third person, and now He turns and speaks to the Prophet ﷺ about them as *My servants*. The command is not "warn them" or "argue with them" — it is *bashshir*, announce good news. That is the tone of the whole passage.

## Ayah 18: the intelligence of the believer

This is the heart of the passage, and it is where the commentators go deepest. "Those who listen to the Word and follow the best thereof — those are the ones whom Allah has guided, and those are men of understanding."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that **several views** have been expressed by learned commentators on what *al-qawl* ("the Word", "what is said") means here. Two of them are worth having.

**First view — al-qawl means the Qur'an.** This is the reading Ibn Kathir opts for, and Maulana Ashraf 'Ali Thanavi went by it too. On this view, *al-qawl* is the Qur'an, the Word of Allah — or the Qur'an inclusive of the teachings of the Prophet ﷺ — and all of it is the best. Ibn Kathir glosses "listen to the Word and follow the best thereof" as **"those who understand it and act in accordance with it."** Hearing is not the point; comprehension issuing in action is.

But then a question arises, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it sharply. If all of the Qur'an is best, the obvious thing to say would have been simply *"who listen to what is said, then follow it."* Why add **aḥsan** — "the best of it"? The answer given is that the extra word tells you *how* they follow: not with "any lack of discernment as is the way of some common people who hear something from someone and start following it without any inquiry, deliberation or insight." These are believers who followed the Word of Allah and the teachings of His Messenger ﷺ *after having found it true and best*. Their obedience is not inherited reflex; it is examined conviction. That is precisely why the verse crowns them at the end as **ulu'l-albāb** — the people of understanding, "the wise, the farsighted, and the discerning ones."

Ibn Kathir supports this reading with a parallel from the Qur'an itself. When Allah gave Musa, peace be upon him, the Tawrah, He said: *"Hold unto these with firmness, and enjoin your people to take the better therein"* (7:145). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that there too, *aḥsan* means the entire Torah and its injunctions — so here likewise, "following the best" means following the entire Qur'an, which is itself referred to as *aḥsan al-ḥadīth*, the best thing said.

**A refinement within this first view.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some elders added a further layer: within the Qur'an itself there are many injunctions that have degrees of *ḥasan* (good) and *aḥsan* (better, best). Retaliation and pardon are both permissible, but pardon is better and more graceful — "and that you be patient is better for you" (4:25). And forgiving is called closer to taqwa — "and it is closer to taqwa that you forgive" (2:237). There are many matters in which a **concession** (*rukhṣah*) has been granted, yet opting for the way of courage and determination (*ʿazīmah*) is still called better and more graceful. On this reading, these are people who listen to the injunctions of the Qur'an — those of concession as well as those of determination — and elect the course of determination; and wherever they face a choice between two things, one good and the other better, they invariably elect the better.

Those two Arabic terms are worth keeping. *Rukhṣah* is the concession — the lighter option; *ʿazīmah* is the way of courage and determination. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, these are matters in which one may take what one likes "without any apprehension of sin" — yet one of the two is pointed out as the more graceful. The verse praises the person whose instinct, when both doors are open, is toward the higher one.

**Second view — al-qawl means whatever people say.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that many commentators take *al-qawl* here to mean what is said by people in general: things about tawhid and shirk, kufr and Islam, *ḥaqq* (truth) and *bāṭil* (falsehood), and even the finer gradations within the truth — good, better, weightier and outweighed. On this reading the verse says: as far as *listening* goes, these people listen to what everyone has to say — disbeliever or believer, truth or falsehood, good or bad. But when it comes to *following*, they follow only that which is the best. So they follow tawhid, not shirk; truth, not falsehood; and where they must choose between degrees of truth, they follow that which is better and weightier.

This is exactly the biography of Salman and Abu Dharr as Qurtubi describes it — men who listened to people of different religions and saw their ways of life, and then chose. And it explains why the verse credits them with **two** attributes, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out: (1) *"those are the ones whom Allah has guided"* — so they did **not** go astray after having listened to so many different things; and (2) *"those are the ones who possess understanding"* — they are sensible people, and their good sense, insight and discernment help them draw the line between good and bad, true and false.

Ibn Kathir's own gloss on those two closing phrases is brief and worth quoting: "those are whom Allah has guided" means they are the ones Allah guided **"in this world and the Hereafter"**; and *ulu'l-albāb* means **"they possess sound reasoning and an upright nature."** Sound reasoning *and* an upright nature — the Qur'an's picture of intelligence is never bare cleverness. It is a clear mind sitting on a sound disposition.

**Holding the two views together.** The commentators genuinely differ here, and the difference is one of scope rather than contradiction. Read one way, the verse praises the believer's discernment *inside* revelation; read the other, it praises his discernment *among* the competing voices around him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents both without declaring either invalid, and a reader is well served by carrying both: examine before you follow, and once you follow, reach for the better of what you are given.

## Ayah 19: the one you cannot rescue

Then the passage turns, and the turn is abrupt: *"Is, then, one against whom the Word of punishment is justified [equal to the one who avoids evil]? Will you rescue him who is in the Fire?"*

Ibn Kathir renders the sense as Allah saying: **"If He has decreed that someone is to be doomed, can you save him from his misguidance and doom?"** The question is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and it is a question that expects the answer *no*. Ibn Kathir draws the principle out plainly: **no one can guide him apart from Allah, because whomever Allah leaves astray cannot be guided, and whomever He guides cannot be led astray.**

Sit with the placement of this ayah. Immediately after a portrait of people whose ears were open and whose choices were sound, we are shown someone the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself could not pull out. The two are held up side by side deliberately — the very structure of the verse is a comparison ("is, then, one against whom the Word of punishment is justified equal to…?").

For the believer, this cuts two ways at once, and both are healthy. It relieves the caller to Allah of a burden that was never his — you deliver, you do not decide; even the Prophet ﷺ was asked whether he could save the one Allah had decreed to be doomed. And it kills complacency: guidance is not a possession you have secured but something in Allah's hand, which is exactly why ayah 18 says *"those are the ones whom **Allah** has guided."* Their discernment was real, and it was His guidance.

## Ayah 20: rooms above rooms

Against the man in the Fire, the passage sets its final image: *"But those who have Taqwa of their Lord, for them are built lofty rooms, one above another, under which rivers flow."* The passage's own translation renders that opening phrase as "those mindful of their Lord."

The reward is described with unusual architectural precision. Ibn Kathir explains *ghuraf min fawqihā ghuraf mabniyyah* as **"story upon story, solidly-constructed, adorned and high."** Not tents, not shade — built structures, stacked, permanent. And *"under which rivers flow"* means, Ibn Kathir says, that **"the rivers flow wherever the people want them to flow"** — the landscape itself answers to its residents.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir gathers several narrations about these rooms.

'Abdullah bin Al-Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"In Paradise there are rooms whose inside can be seen from the outside, and the outside can be seen from the inside."* A bedouin asked, "Who are they for, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said: **"For those who speak kindly, feed the hungry and stand in prayer at night whilst the people are sleeping."** Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by At-Tirmidhi, who said, "Hasan Gharib."

Look at what the answer names: a kind tongue, food given to the hungry, and prayer at night while the people are sleeping. Nothing spectacular is asked — but nothing dramatic is offered as a substitute for it either.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Sahl bin Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The people of Paradise will look towards each other in raised places of Paradise as you look towards the stars on the horizons of the sky."* The narrator mentioned this to An-Nu'man bin Abi 'Ayyash, who said he heard Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, narrate it as *"As you see the stars on the horizon of the east or the west."* Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded **in the Two Sahihs**.

And Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"The people of Paradise will look towards each other in the raised places of Paradise as you look at the high, bright stars which remain on the horizon. Such will be the difference in superiority which some of them have over others."* They said, "O Messenger of Allah, are those the abodes of the Prophets?" He ﷺ said: **"No, by the One in Whose Hand is my soul, they are the abodes of people who believed in Allah and in the Messengers."** At-Tirmidhi also recorded it and said, "Hasan Sahih."

That last exchange is the passage's quiet climax. The Companions assumed such heights must belong to the Prophets. They were told, under oath, that they are the abodes of people who believed in Allah and in the Messengers — which is to say, the very people described back in ayah 17: those who left the false gods and turned to Allah, and in ayah 18: those who listened and followed the best of what they heard.

**"The promise of Allah — and Allah does not fail in His promise."** Ibn Kathir explains *waʿda'llāh* as meaning that all that has been mentioned here "is what Allah has promised to His believing servants," and closes with the Qur'an's own words that **Allah does not fail in His promise** (3:9). The passage that opened with *"announce the good news"* ends by guaranteeing the news. Between the announcement and the guarantee stands only the life described in ayah 18 — listening well, and following the best.

## Living it

- **Shun the false gods, and turn.** Ayah 17 praises not merely avoiding false objects of worship but refusing to *worship* them — and then filling that space by turning to Allah.
- **Examine, then commit.** Both readings of ayah 18 reject the credulity of the person who "hears something from someone and starts following it without any inquiry, deliberation or insight."
- **When two lawful doors are open, take the better one.** Pardon over retaliation; *ʿazīmah* over *rukhṣah*; the weightier of two truths.
- **Do the three small things.** Speak kindly. Feed someone. Stand in prayer at night while the people are sleeping. Those, the Prophet ﷺ said, are the people the rooms belong to — the rooms whose inside can be seen from the outside.
- **Deliver the message; leave the outcome to Allah.** Ayah 19 lifts from your shoulders a weight that was never yours to carry — and reminds you that your own guidance is from Allah, not your own achievement.

passages.title: Rain, softened hearts, the best discourse
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from something everyone has seen — rain falling, crops greening, then yellowing into brittle stalks — to something only some people experience: a heart that opens to Allah's words and softens at His remembrance. What holds them together is the language of *sending down*: in ayah 21 Allah sends water down from the sky; in ayah 23 He has sent down "the best discourse," the Qur'an. In between, ayah 22 divides humanity into the breast Allah has opened and the heart gone hard.

## The rain, and the greater mercy of storing it (ayah 21)

Ayah 21 opens with a challenge to the eyes: **"Do you not see…"** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah is telling us water *originates in the sky* — as in the ayah, "and We send down pure water from the sky" (25:48). It comes down, settles into the earth, and then Allah "causes it to flow wherever He wills," causing springs great and small to flow as they are needed.

Ibn Kathir records that **Saʿid bin Jubayr and ʿAmir Ash-Shaʿbi** said that all the water on earth has its origins in the sky. Saʿid bin Jubayr added that its origins lie in the snow — snow piles up on the mountains, then settles at the bottom of them, and springs flow out from there.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that ***yanābīʿ*** is the plural of *yanbūʿ*, springs that gush out of the soil.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the storing matters as much as the sending. Sending water down is by itself a great blessing — but the arrangement to *conserve* it underground was crucial too. Without that storage, people would benefit from water only while it rained, or for a few days afterwards; yet life depends on it, and it is the kind of need no one can stay free from even for a day. So Allah did not consider it sufficient simply to send the blessing down. He made elaborate and unique arrangements to keep it: some collects in ditches, ponds, tanks and reservoirs; a huge supply is turned into ice and set upon mountain peaks and ridges — an arrangement that also takes care of the danger of the water going bad; then the ice melts and the water travels through veins in the mountains until it reaches the land and gushes out as streams, all over, on its own, without any human input, finally finding its way through the land as rivulets and rivers. The rest keeps flowing underground, retrievable by digging a well almost anywhere.

The favour, then, is not only that it rains. It is that the rain is *kept for you* — by a system you did not design and cannot replace.

## Green, then yellow, then dust

The ayah then tracks what the water produces:

**"crops of different colours"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as different kinds, differing in form, taste, scent and benefit, brought out from the water that fell from the sky or flowed from the springs in the earth.
