Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds: as crops grow and ripen, their colours keep changing from one to another; and because the colours change, the word *mukhtalifan* ("differing") has been used, grammatically, in the form of a *ḥāl* (state, circumstantial condition) — a form which denotes change. It is not a fixed label but a shifting one.

**"then they wither"** — after being ripe and fresh, Ibn Kathir says, they grow old, and you see them turn yellow once they have dried out.

**"then He makes them broken pieces"** — meaning, they become brittle.

**"Surely in that is a reminder for people of understanding."** Ibn Kathir gives the reminder plainly: this world is exactly like that. Green, fresh and beautiful — then old and ugly. The young man becomes a weak, senile old man, and after all of that comes death. *The blessed one is the one whose state after death will be good.* He points out that Allah often likens the life of this world to this very process, as in: "And put forward to them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it and becomes fresh and green. But later it becomes dry and broken pieces, which the winds scatter" (18:45).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds where the lesson should lead: the whole process — water sent down, conserved, made available so people can raise every sort of crop and tree whose colours change, then yellow and dry until grain separates from chaff — provides proof of the infinite power and wisdom of Allah. These are visible signs that could lead a person to discover the reality behind his own creation, and that in turn could become the means through which one succeeds in recognising his own Creator and Master.

Notice who is addressed: *ūlū al-albāb*, "people of understanding." Ibn Kathir defines them by what they do — those who are reminded by this and who learn the lesson from it. Everyone sees the field yellow. Only some read it.

## Two kinds of hearts (ayah 22)

Ayah 22 turns from the field to the chest, and it does so with a question: *afaman* — "Is he, then, whose breast Allah has opened to Islam, so that he is in light from his Lord…?" The sentence leaves the second half of the comparison unspoken, and Ibn Kathir supplies it: is this person equal to the one who is hard-hearted and far from the truth? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the same way, noting the interrogative particle *afaman*: can a person whose heart has been opened up for Islam — who is on the light coming from his Lord, that is, does everything under it — and another person with a hardened heart be equal? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then says that the contrasting part relating to the hardened heart has been mentioned "in the next verse," with a warning of woeful punishment attached to it.

Ibn Kathir places alongside it a verse that says the same thing in another image: "Is he who was dead and We gave him life and set for him a light whereby he can walk among men — like him who is in darkness from which he can never come out?" (6:122). Ibn Kathir glosses that light as belief and that darkness as disbelief. Note that faith is described as a *light you walk by*, not merely a belief you hold.

### What "opening the breast" actually means

**Sharḥ** literally means to open, to enlarge or to extend, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. *Sharḥ al-ṣadr* is the *capacity* of the heart — its capability to receive and accommodate what comes to it. The sense is that a person's heart becomes capable of learning lessons and receiving benefit by deliberating on the divine signs of creation in the heavens and the earth, and particularly by deliberating on his own creation; and the same holds for the other signs of Allah revealed in the form of scriptures and injunctions — the heart has to have the ability to deliberate on them and be benefited by them.

That is precisely why this ayah follows ayah 21. The rain-and-harvest sign has just been laid out. Whether it lands as a *reminder* or as scenery depends entirely on whether the chest is open.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets against this the contrasting case: a heart that is straightened or hardened. It cites the Qur'an's own words, that Allah "makes his heart narrow, much too narrow" (6:125), and the words of this very passage, "woe to those whose hearts are too hard to remember Allah" (39:22) — both standing in contrast to *sharḥ al-ṣadr*, which it defines as a heart opened to the acceptance of truth and at ease with it.

### The Prophet's ﷺ own explanation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits a narration from **Sayyidunā ʿAbdullah Ibn Masʿūd** (may Allah be pleased with him): when the Prophet ﷺ recited this ayah, they asked him what *sharḥ al-ṣadr* means. He ﷺ said that **when the light of īmān (faith) enters the human heart, it enhances its capacity** — which is what makes the comprehension and implementation of Allah's commandments easy for that person. They asked, "O Messenger of Allah, what is the sign of it?" He ﷺ said:

> "Longing passionately for the eternal home, and seeking refuge from the deceptive abode, and preparing for death before its arrival."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this from *al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak* and *al-Baihaqi in Shuʿab-ul-Īmān*, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī.

That answer is testable. He ﷺ did not give a feeling as the sign, nor a mood in worship, but three orientations of a life: what you long for, what you are wary of, and what you are getting ready for.

### The hardened heart

Then: **"So woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah."** Ibn Kathir explains: they do not become soft when Allah is mentioned, they do not feel humility or fear, and they do not understand. "They are in plain error."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the word: *al-qāsiyah* derives from *qasāwah*, which means to be hard-hearted, to have no mercy for anyone, and also describes the one who remains totally unaffected by the need to remember Allah and follow His injunctions. Notice that hardness shows itself in two directions at once: unmoved *upward* toward Allah, and unmerciful *outward* toward people.

## The best discourse (ayah 23)

**"Allah has sent down the best discourse — a Book, its parts resembling one another, oft-repeated."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points back a few ayat: Allah had just described His faithful servants as those "who listen to what is said, then follow the best of it" (39:18). Here, in ayah 23, we are told that the whole Qur'an is *aḥsan al-ḥadīth*, the best of what is said. The word *ḥadīth* means, literally, the speech or account that is related. The outcome of calling the Qur'an *aḥsan al-ḥadīth* is that, out of everything human beings say or relate, the Qur'an remains the most eloquent.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then lists the attributes the ayah gives it:

**1. *Mutashābihan* — a Book whose subjects resemble one another.** Here *mutashābih* means resembling each other, mutually corresponding: the Qur'an's subjects are related to one another and similar, so much so that one ayah gets to be explained or confirmed by another. This word is free of contradiction and conflict.

**2. *Mathānī* — oft-repeated.** The plural of *mathnā*, "repeated": a subject is taken up repeatedly in the Qur'an to help make it settle down in one's mind.

Ibn Kathir gathers the early explanations of this pair:

- **Mujahid**: the entire Qur'an's parts resemble each other and are oft-repeated.
- **Qatadah**: one ayah resembles another, and one letter resembles another.
- **Ad-Dahhak**: it is oft-repeated so that people will understand what their Lord tells them.
- **ʿIkrimah and Al-Hasan**: there may be an ayah in one surah and another ayah in a different surah that resembles it.
- **Saʿid bin Jubayr, narrating from Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him): oft-repeated means that parts of the Qur'an resemble one another and repeat one another.
- **Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah** (as some of the scholars said it was narrated from him): sometimes passages refer to one thing and so resemble one another; sometimes they mention a thing *and its opposite* — believers then disbelievers, Paradise then Hell — and this is the meaning of oft-repeated. Ibn Kathir gives examples: "Verily the most righteous will be in delight; and verily the most wicked will be in the blazing Fire" (82:13–14); the record of the most wicked in *Sijjīn* followed by the record of the most righteous in *ʿIlliyyīn* (83:7–18); and the good final return of the people of taqwā followed by the evil final return of those who transgress (38:49–55). Where a passage is about one thing with parts resembling others, that is "its parts resembling each other."

Ibn Kathir then draws a distinction the reader should keep: *this* "resembling" is **not** the *mutashābihāt* of "In it are ayat that are entirely clear, they are the foundations of the Book; and others not entirely clear" (3:7). That verse, he says, refers to something else altogether.

### Shiver, then soften

**"The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver from it; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah."**

Ibn Kathir explains this as the description of the righteous when they hear the Words of the Compeller, the Protector, the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving, because they understand the promises and warnings contained in them: the frightening words and threats make their skin shiver from fear — and then their skin and their heart soften, *because of their hope for His mercy and kindness*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the same two movements as two effects of one recitation: the Allah-fearing become so overwhelmed and apprehensive before the greatness of Allah that reciting the Qur'an grips them with an awe that makes their hair stand on end; then they hear the ayat promising mercy and forgiveness, which takes them to a state where their bodies and hearts turn tender, mellowed in the remembrance of Allah. Note the sequence in the ayah itself — *thumma*, "then". Awe is not the destination; it is the doorway, and the room it opens into is *dhikr*. This is the exact reverse of ayah 22, described in the same vocabulary: those hearts *do not soften* when Allah is mentioned; these do.

### How the Companions received it

Ibn Kathir lists three ways the righteous are unlike the wicked, immoral sinners here. **First**, they listen to the recitation of the ayat, while those others listen to poetic verse recited by female singers. **Second**, when the ayat of Ar-Rahman are recited to them they fall down in prostration weeping, with the proper attitude of fear, hope, love, understanding and knowledge — as Allah describes the believers, who feel fear in their hearts when Allah is mentioned and are increased in faith when His ayat are recited to them (8:2–4), and who, when reminded of their Lord's ayat, "fall not on them as if they were deaf and blind" (25:73). They are not too busy to pay attention; they listen, understand the meanings, act upon them, and prostrate out of understanding — not out of ignorance and blind following of others.

**Third**, they adhere to the correct etiquette while listening, as the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) used to do when they heard the words of Allah recited by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Their skin would shiver and their hearts would soften to the remembrance of Allah — yet, Ibn Kathir stresses, **they did not shout or do other actions that are not natural**. On the contrary, they would sit quietly with the proper attitude of fear, in an unparalleled fashion, and they attained the victory of praise from their Lord in this world and the Hereafter.

Ibn Kathir supports this with a report from ʿAbdur-Razzaq, from Maʿmar, that **Qatadah** (may Allah have mercy on him) recited this ayah and said: this is the characteristic of the friends of Allah — He has described them in this manner, saying that their *skin shivers, their eyes weep, and their hearts find rest to the remembrance of Allah*. He did not say that they lose their minds and swoon; that, Qatadah said, is the characteristic of the followers of innovation, and it comes from Shayṭān.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, records that **Sayyidah Asmāʼ bint Abī Bakr** (may Allah be pleased with her) said this used to be the common emotional state of the noble Companions: when the Qur'an was recited before them, tears would roll down their eyes and their hair would stand on end. It also narrates, again from Qurtubi, from **Sayyidunā ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said that a servant over whose body hair stands on end due to the fear of Allah — Allah forbids the Fire from ever touching his body.

## "That is the guidance of Allah"

The passage closes: **"That is the guidance of Allah; He guides therewith whom He wills. And whomever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide."**

Ibn Kathir ties this directly to the description just given: *this* — the shivering skin, the softened heart, the composed reverence — is the characteristic of those whom Allah has guided; and anyone who does anything different is one of those whom Allah has sent astray. Guidance is not only a creed one professes; it has a texture, and the ayah has just described it. And the last clause closes every other door: if Allah sends a person astray, there is no guide for him at all. Which is why the sound response here is not self-congratulation but asking — of the One who opens breasts — to be given an opened one.

## Living it

**Read the world.** Ayah 21 asks you to look at rain, at a green field going yellow, and to let it say two things: Allah's power and wisdom are infinite, and you are the crop. Ibn Kathir says the blessed one is the one whose state *after* death is good — the only part of the harvest you still have a say in.

**Watch your own chest.** The Prophet's ﷺ three signs are the check: longing for the eternal home, wariness of the deceptive abode, and preparing for death before it arrives. If a heart is hardening, ayah 22 names the symptom exactly — Allah is mentioned and nothing moves: no softening, no humility, no fear, no understanding.

**Sit with the Qur'an the way they did.** Expect it to work in two motions: awe first, then softness. And take the Companions' manner as the standard — quiet, weeping, attentive, understanding what is said — rather than any louder performance, which Qatadah called the way of the people of innovation.

passages.title: Shielding the face; earlier nations destroyed
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat close the argument against those who reject the Messengers by showing where that rejection ends — first in a single unbearable image of the Day of Resurrection (ayah 24), then in the record of nations who were destroyed for exactly this sin (ayah 25), and finally in the comparison that puts both together: what those nations tasted in this world was real, but it was the smaller of the two punishments (ayah 26). What holds the passage together is a single verb that runs through all three ayat — *tasting*. The wrongdoer is told to *taste* what he earned; Allah made the earlier nations *taste* disgrace in this life; and beyond both lies a torment that is greater still.

## Ayah 24: a question with one half deliberately missing

The ayah opens with **أَفَمَن — "Is he then, the one who…"**. It sets up a comparison. But only one side of it is ever spoken. We are shown the man confronting the worst of the punishment with his face on the Day of Resurrection — and then the sentence simply moves on.

Ibn Kathir supplies the unspoken half: *"Is this like the one who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?"* And he shows that the Qur'an uses this same figure elsewhere, sometimes stating both halves and sometimes only one:

- *"Is he who walks prone on his face, more rightly guided, or he who walks upright on the straight way?"* (67:22)
- *"The Day they will be dragged on their faces into the Fire (it will be said to them): 'Taste you the touch of Hell!'"* (54:48)
- *"Is he who is cast into the Fire better or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?"* (41:40)

Ibn Kathir then makes a precise remark about the style: **"In each of these Ayat, it was sufficient to refer to one of the two groups."** In other words, the omission is not carelessness — it is rhetoric. Describe one man's condition vividly enough and no listener needs to be told what the alternative looks like. The mind completes the sentence on its own, and a conclusion the listener reaches himself lands harder than one he is handed.

Notice too what the three passages Ibn Kathir gathers here have in common: in each of them, the **face**. Walking prone on the face, dragged on the faces into the Fire, confronting the torment with the face. The face is what a person presents to the world, and what he most instinctively protects — which is precisely what makes these images land.

## "Shielding himself with his face"

Look at how the passage is rendered: *"who will confront with his face the awful torment"* (Ibn Kathir), *"those who will only have their bare faces to shield themselves"*, *"the one who tries to save himself from the worst punishment with his face"* (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). All of them circle the same act — trying to ward something off, putting a barrier between yourself and the blow.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out exactly this, and it is the heart of the passage. In this life, when a person faces something hurtful, "he tries to fight it off by using his hands and feet as defensive shields to protect his face." That is the ordinary order of things: the limbs are expendable, the face is protected. You take a blow on the forearm to keep it off your eyes.

On that Day, the order is inverted. "The people of Jahannam will not be able to use even their hands and feet to defend themselves. The punishment that comes will fall directly on their faces." And the reason is given: "Even if he wished to ward off the punishment in defense, he would have no option but to use his very face as the shield, **because he would have been thrown in Jahannam with his hands and feet tied**." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān follows the sentence immediately with the only fitting response: *"We seek refuge with Allah from such a fate."*

For this detail, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Qurtubi transmitting from two early authorities of tafsir: **ʿAtā** and **Ibn Zayd**, who said that a person condemned to Jahannam will have his hands and feet tied before being dragged in there. That single explanatory detail is what makes the image coherent rather than merely grotesque. The man is not choosing to lead with his face. He has nothing else left to lead with.

## "Taste what you used to earn"

Ayah 24 does not end with the image. A voice speaks: **ذُوقُوا مَا كُنتُمْ تَكْسِبُونَ — "Taste what you used to earn!"** Ibn Kathir notes that the man "will be rebuked and he and the evildoers like him will be told" this.

Two things in that short sentence deserve attention.

**"Taste."** Punishment described as something *tasted* is intimate rather than external. You do not observe a taste from a distance; it is inside you, unavoidable, immediate. It is the same word in the ayah Ibn Kathir quotes alongside it: *"Taste you the touch of Hell"* (54:48). And it is the same word Allah uses in ayah 26 for what He made the earlier nations taste in this world.

**"What you used to earn."** Not *what has been decided against you*, but *what you earned*. The wording removes any possibility of complaint. Nothing foreign has been imposed on them; what arrives is their own. So the rebuke is not only pain — it is pain accompanied by the clear knowledge of exactly why. That knowledge is itself part of it.

## Ayah 25: the argument moves from the unseen to the witnessed

Someone hearing ayah 24 could dismiss it as a claim about a future no one has seen. Ayah 25 therefore shifts ground entirely — from the Day of Resurrection to what has already happened:

**كَذَّبَ الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ — "Those before them denied."**

Ibn Kathir explains: "the previous generations who denied the Messengers were destroyed by Allah for their sins." The charge in the ayah is denial of the Messengers, and it is the same charge that stands against those the Qur'an is addressing here. The pattern is not new, and neither is its outcome.

Then the phrase that carries the weight: **مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ — the torment came upon them "from directions they perceived not."** It did not arrive from the quarter they had fortified against. It came from where they were not looking — which is to say, from a direction against which planning is impossible. A person can prepare against a threat he can anticipate. Here there was no direction to face.

Ibn Kathir closes the ayah with the conclusion that follows: **"And none had they to protect them from Allah."** Nothing they had stood between them and Him. That is the same helplessness ayah 24 pictured with bound hands, now shown in what actually befell earlier peoples.

Note the echo between the two ayat. In ayah 24 the man cannot shield himself because his hands and feet are tied; in ayah 25 the earlier nations could not shield themselves because the torment came from where they never perceived it. Different scenes, one lesson: *there is no defence against Allah.*

## Ayah 26: two tastings, and which one is greater

**فَأَذَاقَهُمُ اللَّهُ الْخِزْيَ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا — "So Allah made them to taste the disgrace in the present life"** — rendered elsewhere as *"made them taste humiliation in this worldly life."*

Ibn Kathir explains that this happened in two ways at once: "by means of the punishment and revenge which He sent down upon them, **and the rejoicing of the believers for what happened to them**." So it was not only what struck them; it was also how it looked to those who had believed. The peoples who had denied the Messengers ended as the occasion of the believers' relief.

Ibn Kathir then turns the ayah directly on those being addressed, and this is his sharpest point in the whole passage: **"So, let those who are addressed beware, for they have rejected the noblest of the Messengers and the Seal of the Prophets ﷺ."** The logic runs from lesser to greater. If earlier generations were destroyed for denying the Messengers sent to them, what is the position of those who have rejected the noblest of them all? The history in ayah 25 is not offered as information. It is offered as a measurement of their own danger.

Then the passage's final movement: **وَلَعَذَابُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ — "but greater is the torment of the Hereafter."** Ibn Kathir: "what Allah has promised them of severe punishment in the Hereafter is worse than whatever befell them in this world."

This is where the two halves of the passage lock together. What ayah 25 described — nations destroyed by Allah for their sins, disgraced in this life — is real, and it is the *lesser* of the two. The comparison is doing something careful: it takes the most severe thing the listener has evidence of, and tells him it is the smaller term.

## "If only they knew"

The passage ends on **لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ — "if they only knew."**

This is the diagnosis of the whole condition described across the three ayat. The problem was never that the information was unavailable. Messengers came and were denied; earlier generations were destroyed; the warning stood in plain view. The problem is that it never became *knowledge* — the kind that reorders how a person lives. They had it in front of them and did not know it.

That is a sobering note for a reader rather than a distant one, because a person can recite this passage and still not know it in the sense the ayah means.

## Living it

**Shield yourself now, while shielding is possible.** The whole force of ayah 24 rests on a contrast between two moments. In this life a person still has hands and feet — he can put something between himself and the punishment: obedience, repentance, turning back. In that scene, the hands are tied. The window for defence is the one we are currently inside.

**Do not measure safety by how secure things look.** Ayah 25 says the torment came from where they did not perceive it. Every arrangement a person makes for his own security is made against threats he can imagine. Real security is sought from Allah, not built against a list.

**Take the smaller punishment seriously so as to take the greater one seriously.** Ayah 26 sets worldly disgrace and the Hereafter side by side and calls the second *greater*. Anyone moved by what befell those nations is being asked by this ayah to scale that reaction upward.

**Learn Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's response.** Having described the scene, it did not analyse further; it said: *We seek refuge with Allah from such a fate.* That is the correct posture before a passage like this — not curiosity about the mechanics of punishment, but flight toward the One who alone can protect from it. And as Ibn Kathir says of the earlier generations, when it came, "none had they to protect them from Allah." There is no shelter from Him except with Him.

passages.title: Every parable, in a Qur'an without crookedness
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are about how Allah teaches. The Qur'an pauses here to explain its own method. Allah has filled this Book with parables (ayah 27), He has sent it down in clear Arabic with no crookedness in it (ayah 28), and then, immediately, He gives one such parable to show what shirk — associating others with Allah in worship — actually looks like from the inside (ayah 29). The three hold together as a single movement: the claim, the guarantee, and the demonstration.

## Ayah 27: "And indeed We have put forth for men, in this Qur'an every kind of parable"

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase simply. It means: **"We have explained things to mankind in it [the Qur'an] by setting forth examples and parables."** The Qur'an's images are not decoration around the teaching; they *are* the teaching, one of the ways Allah has chosen to make His meaning plain.

**Why parables?** The ayah gives the purpose: *laʿallahum yatadhakkarūn* — "in order that they may remember." Ibn Kathir's reason is worth memorising: **"Because parables bring the meaning closer to people's minds."** A truth about worship, sincerity and divided loyalty is abstract; a slave with several quarrelling owners is not. The parable carries the meaning into the room where the listener already lives.

Ibn Kathir supports this with Allah's words, *"He sets forth for you a parable from yourselves"* (30:28) — which, Ibn Kathir says, means **"so that you may learn it from yourselves."** The lesson is not fetched from some far country. It is drawn from what the listener already is and already knows, so that in understanding the parable he is in fact reading his own life.

## Ayah 28: "An Arabic Qur'an, without any crookedness"

Having said the Book is full of clarifying examples, Allah now guarantees the medium itself: *qurʼānan ʿarabiyyan ghayra dhī ʿiwaj*.

Ibn Kathir explains: **it is in a plain Arabic tongue, with no crookedness, deviation or confusion. It is plain, clear proof.** And then he adds a point that is easy to read past: **"Allah has made it like this and has revealed it like this."** The clarity of the Qur'an is not an accident of the Arabs' eloquence or a happy feature of their language. It is a deliberate divine choice. Allah *made* it straight and *sent it down* straight.

This is why the two ayat belong together. Parables bring the meaning close; straight Arabic makes sure the meaning arrives undistorted. Ibn Kathir's phrase is exact — *plain, clear proof* — and a proof can only do its work if nothing in it can be bent.

**And the purpose here is different from ayah 27.** In ayah 27 the aim was *yatadhakkarūn*, that they remember. Here it is *laʿallahum yattaqūn*, that they have taqwā of Him. Ibn Kathir defines taqwā in this place with beautiful concreteness: it means **"in order that they may heed the warnings contained therein, and strive to attain the promises therein."** Taqwā — often translated "mindfulness of Allah" or "fear of Allah" — is here given as two live movements of the heart: you take the Book's warnings seriously enough to move away from what it warns of, and you take its promises seriously enough to work for them.

So the sequence runs: **clear examples → remembrance → clear language → taqwā.** Understanding is not the destination; it is the road to a changed life.

## Ayah 29: the parable of the two slaves

Then, having announced that He sets forth parables, Allah immediately sets one forth — as if to say, *here, this is what I mean.* Ibn Kathir titles this section **"The Parable of Shirk."**

Two men are placed side by side.

**The first:** *rajulan fīhi shurakāʼu mutashākisūn* — "a man belonging to many partners disputing with one another." Ibn Kathir: **they were disputing concerning that slave in whom they all had a share.** That detail is the whole point. Every one of them has a claim on him, and they do not agree; he cannot satisfy one without failing another. He spends his life divided.

**The second:** *wa rajulan salaman li-rajul* — "a man belonging entirely to one master." Ibn Kathir: **no one owned him except that one man.** One will to serve, one voice to obey, one person to please. Whatever else his life holds, it holds no contradiction.

**Then the question:** *hal yastawiyāni mathalan* — "Are those two equal in comparison?" Ibn Kathir answers plainly: **they are not the same.** Notice that the ayah puts it to the listener as a question rather than simply informing him — the answer is one he can supply himself.

**The meaning of the likeness.** Ibn Kathir spells it out: **"By the same token, the idolator who worships other gods besides Allah and the sincere believer who worships none besides Allah, with no partner or associate, are not equal. What comparison can there be between them?"** He records that **Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid and others said, "This Ayah is the parable of the idolator and the sincere believer."**

The parable does its work by relocating the argument. It does not dispute theology point by point; it asks a man to picture himself as that slave. And notice what it quietly establishes: both figures in the likeness are owned. The human being is a servant either way. The question was never whether you will belong to someone, only whether you will belong to One or be pulled between many.

## "All praise belongs to Allah!"

Then comes *al-ḥamdu lillāh* — and it seems, at first, to arrive from nowhere. Ibn Kathir explains why it is here: **because this parable is so clear and obvious**, Allah says "All the praises and thanks be to Allah!" — **i.e., for establishing proof against them.**

This is a striking note. Allah is praised for the very clarity that leaves the deniers with nothing to say. The parable is so plain that it settles the case — and that settling is itself worth praising. The straightness promised in ayah 28 has just been demonstrated in ayah 29.

## "But most of them know not"

The passage ends on a sober note: *bal aktharuhum lā yaʿlamūn*. Ibn Kathir's gloss makes the connection to what precedes it: **"and for this reason they associate others in worship with Allah."**

Shirk, then, is traced here to a failure of knowledge. The parable has been placed right in front of them, drawn from their own world, in language with no crookedness in it — and still they do not know, and so they set up partners with Allah.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer:

**Read the Qur'an expecting to be reached.** Allah says He has put forth in it **every kind** of parable, deliberately, because — as Ibn Kathir says — parables bring the meaning closer to people's minds. If a passage feels distant, the fault does not lie with the Book that Allah made straight and revealed straight. Sit with it longer, and look for the image it is holding out to you.

**Let understanding become taqwā.** Ibn Kathir's definition is a usable test: after reading, have you heeded any warning it contains, and have you begun striving for anything it promises? If not, the reading has not yet done its work.

**Test your loyalties by the parable.** Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and Mujahid said this is the parable of the idolater and the sincere believer — and its logic reaches any divided heart. A person may say he worships Allah alone while in practice answering to a crowd of masters who do not agree with one another. Ask honestly whose voice you are actually obeying when they conflict.

passages.title: You will all die, and the dispute is settled
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat take the argument of the sūrah out of this world and into the next. Allah has just set out the parable of the slave owned by many quarrelling partners against the slave who belongs to one master alone (ayah 29) — which Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujāhid and others said is the parable of the idolater and the sincere believer. Now He says: every one of you, Prophet and opponents alike, is going to die (ayah 30), and the quarrel you are having about Him will be reopened before Him (ayah 31), where it will be settled once and for all — Hell for the one who lied about Allah and rejected the truth (ayah 32), and everything the heart could ask for, for the one who brought the truth and those who believed him (ayat 33–35). The thread running through all six is a single one: **this argument is not finished here; it is only adjourned.**

## "You will certainly die" — a word chosen with precision

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the exact form of the word in ayah 30: مَيِّتٌ (*mayyit*), with the doubling on the letter *yāʼ*, denotes someone who **will die in the future**; مَيْتٌ (*mayt*), with the *yāʼ* remaining quiescent, denotes someone who has already died. So the ayah is not describing a state but announcing an appointment. The address is to the Holy Prophet ﷺ — he too is to die — and with him his friends and his foes, who will also die.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (from al-Qurṭubī) says the statement has two purposes at once. The first is to alert everyone and persuade them to be concerned about the Hereafter and to be ready to do everything necessary to achieve that goal. The second is more delicate: to make it very clear that the Holy Prophet ﷺ — despite being the most sublime among the creation and the foremost among the prophets — is not exempted from death, **so that people would not differ about this matter after his passing away from this mortal world.**

Ibn Kathir shows how that safeguard was used. Allah's words *"Verily, you will die, and verily, they (too) will die"* are one of the ayat which Abu Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) quoted when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, so that the people would realize that he had really died. Another ayah which he quoted was:

> "Muhammad is no more than a Messenger, and indeed (many) Messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you then turn back on your heels? And he who turns back on his heels, not the least harm will do to Allah; and Allah will give reward to those who are grateful." (3:144)

Read the two together and you see what Abu Bakr was doing. Ayah 30 establishes the fact — the Prophet ﷺ will die. Ayah 3:144 draws the conclusion — the death of the Messenger is not the end of the matter; the one who turns back on his heels does no harm at all to Allah, and Allah will reward those who are grateful.

## Ayah 31: the court where every argument is reopened

Ibn Kathir gives the plain sense of ayah 31: you will certainly depart this world and be gathered before Allah in the Hereafter. There you will dispute the issues of Tawḥīd and shirk before Allah — the very things you disputed over here — and **He will judge between you with truth, and He is the Judge, the All-Knowing.** He will save the sincere believers who worship Him alone, and He will punish the disbelievers who deny His Oneness and associate others in worship with Him.

But Ibn Kathir immediately widens it. Although the ayah speaks about the believers and the disbelievers and how they will dispute in the Hereafter, **it also includes all disputants in this world, for their disputes will come back to them in the Hereafter.**

That widening is not a commentator's guess. It is what the Companions themselves understood, and it frightened them.

**Az-Zubayr's question.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn az-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said that when ayah 31 was revealed, az-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "O Messenger of Allah, will we repeat our disputes?" He ﷺ said, "Yes." Az-Zubayr said, "This is a very serious matter."

Ahmad recorded from az-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām (may Allah be pleased with him) that when this Sūrah was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — *"Verily, you will die, and verily, they (too) will die. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, you will be disputing before your Lord"* — az-Zubayr said, "O Messenger of Allah, will the sins that we committed against others in this world be repeated for us?" He ﷺ said:

> "Yes, they will be repeated until everyone who is entitled will have his rights restored to him."

Az-Zubayr said, "By Allah, it is a very serious matter." Ibn Kathir notes that it was also recorded by at-Tirmidhī, who said "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

Notice what alarmed him. It was not the great questions of belief and disbelief but the ordinary residue of unsettled human claims — *the sins that we committed against others in this world* — that made him say *this is a very serious matter.*

**Who is disputing with whom.** ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) that ayah 31 means the truthful one will dispute with the liar, the oppressed will dispute with the oppressor, the one who is guided will dispute with the one who is misguided, and the weak will dispute with the arrogant. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of the pronoun *innakum* — "surely you" — as including **believers, disbelievers, Muslims, all of them, oppressor or oppressed.** All of them will submit their cases in the court of their Lord, and He will have the right of the oppressed paid back by the oppressor, whether that oppressor is a disbeliever or a believer.

**Even the soul and the body.** Ibn Mandah recorded in *Kitāb ar-Rūḥ* that Ibn ʿAbbās said the people will dispute on the Day of Resurrection to the extent that the soul will dispute with the body. The soul will say to the body, "You did such and such," and the body will say to the soul, "You told me to do it and you tempted me." Then Allah will send an angel to judge between them, and he will say, "You two are like a man who cannot walk but can see, and a man who cannot see but can walk." They went into a garden, and the one who could not walk said to the blind man, "I see fruit there, but I cannot reach it." The blind man said, "Climb on me and get it." So he climbed on him and got it. So which of them is the wrongdoer? They will say, "Both of them." The angel will say to them, "You have passed judgement against yourselves." The body was a means of transportation for the soul.

The point is aimed squarely at the excuse every one of us reaches for. *My desires pushed me. My body's appetites carried me.* On that Day the two halves of the excuse will be standing in the dock together.

**Ibn ʿUmar and the Fitnah.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said that Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "This ayah was revealed and we did not know what it was revealed about." He said, "We said, what will we dispute about? There is no dispute between us and the People of the Book, so what will we dispute about? Until the Fitnah occurred." Then Ibn ʿUmar said, "This is what our Lord promised us we would dispute about." This was recorded by an-Nasāʼī. A generation that had assumed the ayah was about them and their opponents discovered, painfully, that it was about them and each other.

## How the rights will actually be paid back

This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān goes into the mechanics, and it is the most practically urgent part of the passage.

From a narration of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that appears in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī: the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that a person who has a right of someone due against him should either pay it off or have it forgiven **right here in this world**, and so stand absolved of any responsibility on that count. The reason given is stark: there are not going to be any currencies of dirhams and dinars — or any others found in this mortal world — in the universe of the Hereafter. If the oppressor has some good deeds in his account, those deeds will be taken from him to the measure of the oppression he did and given to the oppressed. And in case he has no good deeds with him, the bad deeds and sins of the oppressed will be taken and put into the account of the oppressor.

And from a narration of Abu Hurayrah in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*: the Holy Prophet ﷺ one day asked his noble Companions, "Do you know who a pauper is?" They said, "O Messenger of Allah, as for us, a pauper is one who has neither cash nor the things needed to run one's life." He ﷺ said that the real pauper of his Ummah is a person who will come on the Day of Judgment with lots of good deeds — prayers, fasts, zakāh and things like that — but whose record of dealings with others is such that he had hurled invectives on someone, levelled a false accusation against someone, devoured someone's property by unfair means, had someone killed, beaten or harassed. All those he oppressed will take their plaint before Allah, and the good deeds of the oppressor will be distributed over the oppressed. After that, when no good deeds are left and the claims of the oppressed still remain to be settled, the sins of the oppressed will be passed on to the oppressor, and he will be thrown into Jahannam. A man with everything, who arrives bankrupt.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites Ṭabarānī, citing a trustworthy authority, reporting from Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Holy Prophet ﷺ said the first case presented in the court of Allah will be that of **a man and his wife** — and the tongue will be silent there; instead the hands and feet of the woman will bear witness as to the blames she used to impute to her husband, and the hands and feet of the man will bear witness as to how he used to cause pain to his wife. After that, servants will be brought before their respective masters and redress will be provided for their complaints. After that, people from the common markets with whom one had one dealing or another will be presented, and if one of them has been subjected to some injustice, his right will be duly settled.

That ordering deserves a pause. The first docket in the highest court is not politics or property. It is marriage. Then the people who work for you. Then the ordinary buying and selling you did without a second thought.

## Will faith itself be taken away?

A natural worry follows: if every good deed can be stripped from a wrongdoer, could a believer be stripped of his faith too and left with nothing?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers by quoting *Tafsīr Maẓharī*, which, after reporting all the narrations cited above, states that what is given over in settlement of the rights of the oppressed means deeds **other than īmān** (faith). The reasoning: all oppressions and injustices are acts of sin — they are not kufr, disbelief — and the punishment of sinful deeds will be limited, whereas īmān is a limitless deed and its reward too is limitless: living in Jannah forever, even though that may come after having gone through the punishment of sins and staying in Jahannam for a certain period. So when the good deeds of the oppressor — with the exception of īmān — are finished, given away to the last deed with nothing left behind but īmān, that īmān will not be taken away from him forcibly. Instead, the rights of the oppressed will be paid back by putting the sins of the oppressed into the account of the oppressor. As a result, after he has undergone the punishment of his sins, he will finally enter Jannah, and that state of his will be everlasting. The author of *Tafsīr Maẓharī* says that Imām al-Bayhaqī has also said so.

Two things must be held together here and not played off against each other: the justice is real and terrifying, and īmān is not forfeit. Neither cancels the other.

## Ayah 32: the worst wrongdoer of all

After the courtroom, the verdicts. Ayah 32 asks: *"Then, who does more wrong than one who utters a lie against Allah, and denies the truth when it comes to him!"* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: **there is no one who does more wrong than such a person** — because he combines the two aspects of falsehood at once: disbelief in Allah, and disbelief in the Messenger of Allah. He makes false claims, and then rejects the truth when it reaches him.

Ibn Kathir spells out the lies the idolaters actually uttered: that there were other gods besides Him, that the angels were the daughters of Allah, and that Allah had a son — glorified be He, far above all that they say. Moreover, they rejected the truth when it came to them on the lips of the Messengers (peace and blessings be upon them all). Then comes the threat: *"Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?"* — who are, Ibn Kathir says, the deniers and rejecters.

## Ayah 33: aṣ-ṣidq, and the ones who carried it

Against that stands ayah 33: **"And he who has brought the truth (aṣ-ṣidq) and (those who) believed therein — they are those who have Taqwa."**

Mujāhid, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Ibn Zayd all said: *"The one who brought the truth was the Messenger ﷺ."* ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said that *"And he who has brought the truth"* means the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and *"and (those who) believed therein"* means the Muslims.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word itself. Ayah 32 speaks of the one who **rejects** *aṣ-ṣidq*; ayah 33 of the one who **has come with** *aṣ-ṣidq* — the same word on both sides of the divide, so the whole of humanity is sorted by its response to one thing. And at both these places, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, *aṣ-ṣidq* means the teachings brought by the Holy Prophet ﷺ, whether the Qur'an or his other teachings in the aḥādīth in addition to the Qur'an. The expression *ṣaddaqa bihi* — "and believed it to be true" — **includes all believers who have testified to it**, which means it reaches down the centuries to anyone reading this ayah today and affirming it.

Note also which quality is named for them: not scholars, not warriors, but *al-muttaqūn*, the people of taqwā — the mindfulness of Allah that makes a person careful. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said of them simply: **"They fear and shun Shirk."** Given the parable of the two slaves in ayah 29 that opened this whole run, that is exactly the right definition here.

## Ayat 34–35: the two-sided generosity

Ayah 34: *"They shall have all that they will desire with their Lord."* Ibn Kathir: this means in Paradise — **whatever they ask for they will have.** Set that against the pauper of the hadith who arrives with a mountain of deeds and leaves with nothing: here are people whose account is not merely intact but open-ended. *"That is the reward of the doers of good (al-muḥsinīn)."*

Then ayah 35 explains how such people can be given such a thing, and it works in two directions at once:

- **"So that Allah may expiate from them the evil of what they did"** — the Arabic is *aswa'a alladhī ʿamilū*, which the translation of this passage renders "even the worst of what they did."
- **"and give them the reward, according to the best of what they used to do"** — the reward is measured against the best of their deeds.

The bad is erased; the good is taken at its best and rewarded. Ibn Kathir points to the parallel ayah:

> "They are those from whom We shall accept the best of their deeds and overlook their evil deeds. (They shall be) among the dwellers of Paradise, a promise of truth, which they have been promised." (46:16)

## Living it

The passage does not ask for a feeling; it asks for two concrete things.

**Settle your accounts now.** The instruction in the narration of Abu Hurayrah in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of al-Bukhārī could not be more practical: if you owe someone — money, or an apology, or a reputation you damaged — pay it off or have it forgiven **in this world**, because the currency you would need in the next one does not exist there. Start where the Ṭabarānī narration says the court starts: your spouse, then those who work for you, then the people you deal with in the marketplace.

**And do not despair at the size of it.** The same passage that promises the court also promises ayah 35: the evil expiated, and the reward given according to the best of what they used to do — for the one who brought the truth and everyone who believed him.

Az-Zubayr, hearing all this from the Prophet ﷺ himself, said only: *"By Allah, it is a very serious matter."* It is difficult to improve on that as a response.

passages.title: Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer a threat. Someone has tried to frighten the Prophet ﷺ, and instead of arguing point by point, the Qur'an replies with a question so simple it dismantles the whole threat: **"Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?"** What holds ayat 36–40 together is that single question, pressed from every side — first as a challenge (36), then as a statement about who really controls guidance and retribution (37), then as an argument the opponents themselves cannot escape (38), and finally as a parting of the ways, with each side told to carry on and wait to see how it ends (39–40).

## The moment behind ayah 36

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that this verse was revealed against the background of a specific event. The disbelievers had threatened the Prophet ﷺ and his noble Companions: if they went on treating the idols irreverently, they would never escape the curse of those idols — a fate, they implied, too lethal to risk. The reply came: *Is Allah not sufficient for His slave?*

Ibn Kathir describes the same scene from the wording of the ayah itself: **"Yet they try to frighten you with those besides Him"** means that the idolaters tried to scare the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with their idols and the gods they called upon besides Allah, out of ignorance and misguidance.

Notice how strange the threat is once you name it. They were not threatening him with armies or with their own hands here — they were threatening him with *objects*. And the answer does not even engage the idols. It simply asks whether the One he actually depends on is enough.

## "His servant" — who is meant?

The Arabic is *ʿabdahu*, "His servant." Both commentaries pause here, and the difference is worth understanding.

**Ibn Kathir** notes that some read it in the plural, "His servants," and gives the sense of the ayah as: **Allah is sufficient for the one who worships Him and relies upon Him.** The description fits whoever fills it.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** lays the two positions out side by side. Because of the occasion of revelation, some commentators took "His slave" to mean one particular slave of Allah — the Prophet ﷺ himself; Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi, a summary of whose Tafsir appears in the original edition of Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, opted for this reading. Other commentators took *ʿabd* in its general sense, and another recitation (*qirāʾah*) of the verse — *ʿibādihi*, "His slaves" — supports them. Maʿārif then makes the point that settles the matter for a reader: as for the subject itself, it is general in any case, because Allah is sufficient for every one of His slaves.

So the ayah lands twice. It was consolation to a particular servant under particular threat, and it is a standing promise to anyone who takes up that same position of servanthood and reliance.

Note also what the ayah calls him. Not "His Prophet," not "His Messenger" — **His servant**. The sufficiency is attached to servanthood, and Ibn Kathir's gloss says exactly which servanthood: it is for "the one who worships Him and relies upon Him." Worship and reliance travel together. Sufficiency is not promised to someone who wants Allah's protection while giving his devotion elsewhere.

## Ayah 37: two doors no one else can open

The end of ayah 36 and the start of ayah 37 form a matched pair, and Ibn Kathir treats them as one statement:

> And whom Allah sends astray, for him there will be no guide. And whomsoever Allah guides, for him there will be no misleader.

Two closed doors, in both directions. No one can guide the one Allah leaves in misguidance; no one can drag away the one Allah has guided. If that is so, the people making threats in ayah 36 are not holding the lever they imagine. They cannot pull a guided man off his path — not with idols, not with curses, not with anything.

Then the second rhetorical question: **"Is Allah not Almighty, Possessor of Retribution?"** Ibn Kathir draws out both names, and it is worth noticing whom each one is aimed at:

- Because He is **Almighty** (*ʿAzīz*), "whoever relies on Him and turns to Him will never be forsaken, for He is the Almighty Who cannot be overwhelmed by another." No power exists that could overrule Him on your account.
- Because He is **Possessor of Retribution**, "there is none more severe than Him in exacting retribution on those who disbelieve in Him, associate others in worship with Him, and resist His Messenger ﷺ."

The same two names, in Ibn Kathir's reading, do two jobs at once: they steady the threatened servant and they warn the one doing the threatening.

## Ayah 38: their own answer used against them

Ayah 38 turns from consoling the Prophet ﷺ to arguing with the people threatening him, and it opens by getting them to testify against themselves:

> And verily, if you ask them: "Who created the heavens and the earth?" Surely, they will say: "Allah."

Ibn Kathir explains the point: **the idolaters used to recognise that Allah was the Creator of all things, yet in spite of that they still worshipped others besides Him — others who had no power to bring benefit or cause harm.** Their creed was never that the idols made the universe. Ask them who did, and the word "Allah" comes out of their own mouths.

That admission is the hinge. Having conceded the Creator, they face a question they cannot answer:

> Say: "Tell me then, the things that you invoke besides Allah — if Allah intended some harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended some mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?"

Ibn Kathir's comment is a single flat sentence: **"they cannot do any of that at all."**

Look at how the question is built. It covers both directions at once — pushing away a harm Allah has willed, and holding back a mercy Allah has willed. Everything you fear and everything you hope for is contained in those two. And it is exactly the threat of ayah 36 turned inside out. They had said: *the idols will harm you.* The reply is: can they even move what Allah has decided? Then what is it you think you are frightening me with?

## From the Sunnah: the advice Ibn Kathir places right here

At this point in the passage, Ibn Kathir cites a narration that **Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him,** attributing it to the Prophet ﷺ:

> Be mindful of Allah and He will protect you; be mindful of Allah and you will find Him ever with you. Turn to Allah in times of ease and He will turn to you in times of difficulty. If you ask anyone for anything, then ask Allah; if you seek help from anyone, then seek help from Allah. Know that even if the entire nation were to come together to do you some harm that Allah has not decreed for you, they will never be able to harm you; and if they were to come together to do you some good that Allah has not decreed for you, they will never be able to do that. The pages have dried and the pens have been lifted. Strive for the sake of Allah with thankfulness and firm conviction, and know that in patiently persevering with regard to something that you dislike there is much goodness. Victory comes with patience, a way out comes from difficulty, and with hardship comes ease.

This is the ayah's argument turned into a way of living. The ayah asked whether the idols could remove a harm or withhold a mercy; the narration widens the question to *the entire nation* — every human being acting together — and returns the same verdict in both directions. Harm and benefit that Allah has not written simply do not arrive: "the pages have dried and the pens have been lifted."

Two things keep this from collapsing into fatalism. First, it is paired with action — *be mindful of Allah, ask Him, seek help from Him, strive with thankfulness and firm conviction.* Second, it is paired with patience, because the narration never promises that nothing painful will happen. It promises that nothing happens outside His decree, that there is much good in patiently bearing what you dislike, and that relief is on its way: victory with patience, a way out from difficulty, ease with hardship.

## "Ḥasbiya Allāh" — the answer placed on the servant's own tongue

The question of ayah 36 — *Is Allah not sufficient?* — is finally answered inside ayah 38, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to say it himself:

> **Say: "Sufficient for me is Allah; in Him those who trust must put their trust."**

Ibn Kathir's gloss on *ḥasbiya Allāh* is as plain as it gets: **"Allah is enough for me."** Not *Allah will help me alongside my other supports* — enough. And the sentence does not stop with the Prophet ﷺ; it opens outward: *let all those who trust put their trust in Him.* That is *tawakkul*, reliance — leaning your weight on Allah instead of on whatever is being waved in your face.

Ibn Kathir sets this beside the words of the Prophet **Hud**, peace be upon him, whose people had made the very same kind of threat — that some of their gods had seized him with evil. His reply (quoted by Ibn Kathir from Surah Hud, 11:54–56) was not defensive at all:

> "I call Allah to witness, and bear you witness, that I am free from that which you ascribe as partners in worship with Him. So plot against me, all of you, and give me no respite. I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord! There is not a moving creature but He has the grasp of its forelock. Verily, my Lord is on the straight path."

The same accusation, the same answer, generations apart. And the image repays sitting with: there is not a moving creature but He has the grasp of its forelock. The thing they are threatening you with is itself being held.

## Ayat 39–40: "carry on, then — and you will see"

Once the argument is exhausted, the passage closes the conversation:

> Say: "O my people! Work according to your way; I am working. Then you will come to know — to whom comes a disgracing torment, and on whom descends an everlasting torment."

Ibn Kathir reads **"Work according to your way"** as *a threat and a warning*, not permission. **"I am working"** means: according to my way. **"Then you will come to know"** means: you will learn the consequences.

There is a certain dignity in this. No pleading and no bluster — a clean separation, with the matter left to be settled by outcome rather than by argument. And notice the address: *O my people.* Even at the point of parting, he still calls them his own.

Ayah 40 names what they will come to know, and Ibn Kathir separates the two punishments carefully:

- **"a disgracing torment"** — this one, he says, is *in this world*. Its very quality is humiliation: the men who threatened the Prophet ﷺ with ruin at the hands of their idols are told where disgrace actually falls.
- **"an everlasting torment"** — "ongoing and eternal, with no escape," and it comes on the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Kathir breaks off his commentary at that line to add: *We seek refuge with Allah from that.* That is the right response, and worth borrowing. This is not information to be filed away; it is something to seek refuge from.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns against one particular way of wasting this passage. Readers, it says, tend to pass over *"And they are frightening you of those [false gods whom they worship] other than Him"* as though it concerned only a particular event — the threats of the disbelievers and the blessed person of the Prophet ﷺ — and so they never exert themselves enough to find the guidance it holds for us.

But the shape of the situation recurs constantly. Maʿārif spells it out: anyone who threatens a Muslim on the ground that, if he does not commit some forbidden act or sin, the superiors at whose mercy he is will be displeased with him and may even hurt him — that person too comes under this ayah, even when the one threatening and the one threatened are both Muslims. It observes that this happens all over the world, in most jobs people do, leaving a person facing a dilemma: contravene the divine laws he is bound by, or become the target of a superior officer's wrath.

The guidance Maʿārif draws is unsentimental. Resolve that you will abstain from sin exclusively for the sake of Allah. Then do not care about any officer or authority asking you to act counter to the divine laws — and the help and support of Allah will be with you. The worst that can happen is that you lose that job; Allah will make some other arrangement for your sustenance. Maʿārif even notes what is typical of a believer in the meantime: he keeps trying to find a suitable job elsewhere, so that he is placed in a position to leave immediately.

That is this passage in working clothes. Whatever is being held over you draws all of its power from your belief that it can bring you a harm or withhold from you a good. Ayah 38 asks whether it can do either. And ayah 36 asks the only question left once the answer is no: **Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?**

passages.title: Souls in Allah's hand; intercession is His
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat answer a single question: **who is actually in control?** The Prophet ﷺ is told that his job is to deliver the Book, not to force hearts open (41); Allah then shows that He holds every soul in His hand, taking it in death and taking it again every night in sleep (42); and from that follows the verdict on the idols the pagans were leaning on — powerless things that cannot intercede, because all intercession belongs to the One who owns the heavens and the earth (43–44). Control of the soul and control of intercession are the same point made twice: nothing and no one stands between you and Allah except by His leave.

## Ayah 41 — the Book is for everyone; the outcome is not on you

A little context first. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a few ayat earlier, at ayah 36, Allah had asked: *"Is Allah not sufficient for (the protection of) His slave?"* That was revealed against the background of an event: the disbelievers had threatened the Prophet ﷺ and his noble Companions that if they acted irreverently against the idols, they would never escape the curse of those idols. The reply was that Allah alone suffices. (Maʿārif adds that commentators differed over *ʿabdahu*, "His slave": some — including Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi — read it as one particular servant, the Prophet ﷺ; others take "slave" in its general sense, supported by another *qirāʾah*, or recitation, of the word as *ʿibādihi*, "His slaves". Maʿārif observes that the subject is general in any case, since Allah is sufficient for every one of His slaves.)

Hold that scene in mind and ayah 41 lands differently. A man under threat is now told exactly what he is and is not responsible for.

*"Verily, We have sent down to you the Book"* — Ibn Kathir says plainly: **meaning, the Qur'an**. *"for mankind in truth"* — and here he widens it: **for all of creation, mankind and Jinn, so that he may warn them therewith**. This is not a message for a tribe or a generation.

Then the two halves of the human response, and where each lands:

- *"So, whosoever accepts the guidance, it is only for himself"* — Ibn Kathir: **the benefit of that will return to him.**
- *"and whosoever goes astray, he goes astray only for his (own) loss"* — **the consequences of that will return to him.**

Notice how the ayah is built. Guidance and misguidance are not favours done to the Messenger or injuries inflicted on him. Each person's choice curls back on the one who made it. That is why the ayah ends: *"And you are not a trustee over them."*

**"Trustee" — wakīl.** Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase: **"you are not responsible for guiding them."** He then brings two other ayat to fix the meaning:

- *"But you are only a warner. And Allah is a Trustee over all things"* (11:12) — the very word denied here to the Prophet ﷺ is, in that ayah, affirmed for Allah.
- *"your duty is only to convey and on Us is the reckoning"* (13:40).

So the messenger's portion is *balāgh* — conveying, delivery; the reckoning is Allah's. This is one of the great mercies of the passage, and it is aimed first at the most sincere caller who ever lived. If the Prophet ﷺ was not made answerable for whether people accepted, no one after him is either.

## Ayah 42 — Allah takes the soul twice

Ibn Kathir introduces this ayah by telling us that Allah **is in control of all things and does as He wills**, and he sets out a striking pairing: Allah causes men to die **the "greater death"** when He sends the angels to take their souls from their bodies, and He causes them to **"die a lesser death"** when they sleep.

He then quotes 6:60–61, where the same two deaths appear in the reverse order — *"It is He, Who takes your souls by night (when you are asleep), and has knowledge of all that you have done by day, then He raises (wakes) you up again that a term appointed be fulfilled… He is the Irresistible, over His servants, and He sends guardians (angels…) over you, until when death approaches one of you, Our messengers (angels) take his soul, and they never neglect their duty."* Ibn Kathir points out the sequence deliberately: **there, the lesser death then the greater death after it; here in 39:42, the greater then the lesser.** Between the two passages the whole of a human life is enclosed — the nightly taking and the final one — with nothing outside Allah's grip.

### The word: *tawaffā*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the key verb. **تَوَفَّى (tawaffā) literally means to receive, to take back, to exact.** The Qur'an does not say Allah "kills" the souls here; it says He *takes them back*. That single word carries the doctrine: souls are not our property, they are held and recalled by their Owner.

Maʿārif states the point without hedging: in this ayah Allah has stated very clearly and emphatically that the spirits or souls (*arwāḥ*) of living beings are under His free will and discretionary dispensation **at all times and under all conditions** — He can seize, exact and take them back at will. And there is at least one manifestation of this that every living being sees and feels every day: once asleep, the *rūḥ* is, so to say, taken away from the body, then returned on rising from sleep — and ultimately one such time is bound to come when this *rūḥ* stands seized, absolutely and conclusively, after which it will never be returned.

Maʿārif adds a technical note: in this ayah *yatawaffā* is used in the sense of *qabḍ* ("takes in full") by way of **ʿumūm al-majāz** — a broad figurative usage that covers both meanings, the sleeping case and the dying case, in one word.

### What "taking the soul" means

Citing **Tafsīr Maẓharī**, Maʿārif explains that the sense of "taking the *rūḥ* away" is to sever its connection with the human body, and this happens in degrees:

1. **Totally severed, both outwardly and inwardly** — this is what death is.
2. **Severed only outwardly while it remains active inwardly** — this is sleep. What is severed is sense and volitional movement, the obvious signs of life; the connection of the *rūḥ* with the body remains active inwardly, so one breathes and stays alive. In that state the human spirit is made to turn its attention to the *ʿālam al-mithāl*, the "universe of images", and is made to pass into a state of forgetfulness and suspension away from this universe — so that one can become fully at rest.

And then, Maẓharī adds, at times even this inward connection is severed, at which the life of the body goes extinct totally.

That reframes sleep. It is not simply the body powering down; it is a nightly withdrawal of the soul, a small death and a small return, granted so we can rest.

### Sayyidnā ʿAlī on sleep and dreams

Maʿārif says this distinction also finds support in a saying of Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him): at the time of sleep the *rūḥ* goes away from the body, **but a beam or ray of it stays behind**, and because of that one remains alive — and it is through that "beamed" connection that one sees a dream.

He adds a criterion for dreams: a dream seen in the state where the attention of the *rūḥ* was raptly turned toward the universe of images is a **true dream**; but if it is seen while the *rūḥ* is returning back to the body, it becomes polluted with Shaitanic inputs and no longer remains a true dream. And he also said that the *rūḥ* which leaves the body during sleep returns to it on waking **within a time much less than an eye would take to wink**.

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir says the ayah's wording indicates that the souls **meet in the higher realm**, as was stated in a hadith attributed to the Prophet ﷺ which was narrated by **Ibn Mandah and others**.

He then reports what is **in the Two Sahihs of Al-Bukhari and Muslim**, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "When anyone of you goes to bed, let him brush down the bed with his garment, for he does not know what has come on his bed since he left it. Then let him say, *In Your Name, O Lord, I lay down my side and in Your Name I raise it up; if You take my soul, have mercy on it, and if You send it back, protect it with that which You protect Your righteous servants.*"

Look at how exactly this duʿāʾ tracks the ayah. Allah *keeps* some souls and *sends back* others — and the sleeper asks for the right thing under each outcome: **mercy** if it is taken, **protection** if it is sent back. Every night a Muslim is taught to lie down as one who may not wake, and to hand the soul over deliberately rather than have it taken from him unaware.

### He does not make mistakes

On *"He keeps those (souls) for which He has ordained death and sends the rest for a term appointed"*, Ibn Kathir explains that He keeps those which have died and returns the others back for an appointed term, and reports:

- **As-Suddī**: "For the rest of their lives."
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him): "He keeps the souls of the dead and sends back the souls of the living, **and He does not make any mistakes.**"

Ibn ʿAbbās's remark is quietly enormous. Souls are withdrawn and returned every night; not one is misplaced, not one held past its appointed hour or released before it.

The ayah closes: *"Verily, in this are signs for a people who think deeply."* — *yatafakkarūn*, those who reflect. The sign is not hidden in a distant heaven; it is in your own bed, every night, if you will think about it.

## Ayat 43–44 — all intercession belongs to Allah

Now the argument turns. If Allah alone takes and returns the soul, what exactly were the idolaters expecting from their idols?

Ayah 43 asks: *"Have they taken as intercessors besides Allah?"* Ibn Kathir says Allah **condemns the idolators for taking intercessors besides Allah, namely the idols and false gods whom they have taken on the basis of their own whims, with no evidence or proof.** Then comes the demolition in the second half of the ayah: *"Say: 'Even if they have power over nothing whatever and have no intelligence?'"* Ibn Kathir spells out what these objects actually are: **they are not able to do anything; they have no minds with which to think, and they cannot hear or see. They are inanimate and are much worse off than animals.**

That last comparison is deliberately humiliating. An animal at least perceives and moves. The thing being asked to plead your case before the Lord of the worlds is below the animal — and an intercessor who cannot hear your request, cannot understand it, and has no power to act on it is no intercessor at all.

Ayah 44 replaces the false picture with the true one: *"Say: 'To Allah belongs all intercession.'"* Ibn Kathir explains the instruction to the Prophet ﷺ — say to those people who claim they have taken intercessors with Allah that **intercession is of no avail except for the one with whom Allah is pleased and to whom He has granted permission to intercede. The whole matter rests with Him.** He anchors this with Āyat al-Kursī: *"Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?"* (2:255).

This is the balanced position the passage teaches. Intercession is not abolished — it is **owned**. It belongs entirely to Allah; it happens only where He permits it and only for the one He is pleased with. It is never a lever a creature can pull on Allah, and it is exactly what the idolaters were condemned for seeking from those besides Him.

The rest of ayah 44 supplies the reason: *"His is the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth"* — Ibn Kathir: **He is the One Who is in control of all that** — *"Then to Him you shall be brought back"*: **on the Day of Resurrection, then He will judge between you with His justice, and He will reward or punish each person according to his deeds.**

Read the passage's chain in one breath: He owns your soul (42), He owns the heavens and the earth (44), and the whole matter of intercession rests with Him (44) — so the return is to Him and the judgement is His. There is no side door.

## Living it

**Carry the message; do not carry the verdict.** Ayah 41 assigns the caller his portion — conveying — and reserves the reckoning for Allah. Say the truth to your family, your colleagues, your children; then release the result. You were never made a *wakīl* over anyone's heart.

**Let the threats lose their grip.** Maʿārif draws a practical lesson from the setting of ayah 36. It observes that readers generally pass by *"they are frightening you of those other than Him"* as if it concerned only that one event, and so do not exert themselves to find the guidance in it. But anyone who is threatened that unless he commits a *ḥarām* act his superiors — at whose mercy he is — will be displeased and may even hurt him is also included under this verse, even when both parties are Muslims. Maʿārif says this happens all over the world, in most jobs, and gives the guideline: **resolve to abstain from sin exclusively for the sake of Allah, then do not care about any officer or authority asking you to act counter to the Divine laws; the help and support of Allah will be with you.** The worst that can happen is losing that job — and Allah will make some other arrangement for your sustenance. Maʿārif adds that it is typical of a believer to keep looking for a suitable job elsewhere, so that he is in a position to leave immediately.

**Sleep as a Muslim sleeps.** Take ayah 42 to bed with you. Brush down the bedding as the Prophet ﷺ taught, and say the words he taught — asking for mercy if the soul is taken and protection if it is sent back. Whatever you would regret leaving unsettled if the soul were kept tonight, settle it before you lie down.

**Take your needs to the Owner.** Ayat 43–44 close every door but one. Whatever cannot hear, cannot understand, and has no power can do nothing for you on the Day you are brought back. Ask the One to whom all intercession belongs, who owns the heavens and the earth, and who — as Ibn ʿAbbās said of the souls He holds — does not make any mistakes.

passages.title: Hearts that shrink when Allah alone is named
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from a diagnosis to a prescription. Ayah 45 exposes what idolatry does to a heart — when Allah alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter are filled with disgust, while the mention of others besides Him makes them rejoice. Ayah 46 then hands the Prophet ﷺ, and every believer after him, the exact opposite of that heart: a supplication that calls on Allah alone with no partner, by His names, and leaves every disputed matter to His judgement. Ayat 47 and 48 show where that first heart ends up on the Day when the judgement finally falls.

What holds the passage together is one question: **where does your heart go when Allah alone is named?** Everything else — the refused ransom, the exposed deeds, the mockery closing in — follows from the answer.

## The setting: intercessors who cannot hear

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 45 as the climax of what came just before it. In ayat 43–44 Allah condemns the idolaters for taking intercessors besides Him — idols and false gods adopted, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "on the basis of their own whims, with no evidence or proof." He describes these objects of worship starkly: they are not able to do anything; they have no minds with which to think; they cannot hear or see. They are inanimate, and — in his words — much worse off than animals.

The answer given in ayah 44 is that **all** intercession belongs to Allah. Ibn Kathir explains it as an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ: tell these people that intercession is of no avail except for the one with whom Allah is pleased and to whom He has granted permission to intercede. The whole matter rests with Him. He supports this by citing *"Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?"* (2:255). And *"His is the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth"* means, in his words, that He is the One Who is in control of all that — after which *"Then to Him you shall be brought back"* means the Day of Resurrection, when He will judge between people with His justice and reward or punish each person according to his deeds.

So intercession is not denied; it is relocated. It is not a private influence some being holds over Allah — it is a permission Allah grants. Once that is settled, ayah 45 asks how a person reacts to that settlement.

## Ayah 45: the heart that shrinks

*"And when Allah Alone is mentioned…"* — Ibn Kathir spells out what that mention actually is: **"when it is said there is no (true) deity except Allah Alone."**

The verb the Qur'an uses is *ishma'azzat*. Ibn Kathir's rendering is that their hearts are **filled with disgust**, and Mujahid, whom he cites here, explained that phrase as: **"they recoil in horror."** Notice where the verse locates this: in the *hearts*. It is not described as something said out loud.

Ibn Kathir places beside it a verse from another sūrah: *"Truly, when it was said to them: 'Lā ilāha illā Allāh,' they puffed themselves up with pride"* (37:35) — which, he says, means **they were too proud to follow it.** Then comes one of his most piercing lines on this passage: their hearts could not accept anything good, **and whoever cannot accept good will accept evil.** A heart is not neutral. If it is sealed against the truth, it does not stay empty; it fills with the alternative.
