**The other half of the test.** The verse does not stop at the recoiling. *"And when those besides Him are mentioned, behold, they rejoice!"* Ibn Kathir identifies "those besides Him" as the idols and false gods — he notes this was the view of Mujahid — and glosses *yastabshirūn* simply as: **they feel happy.** So the ayah takes two readings from the same instrument. Pure tawḥīd (declaring Allah's oneness, with no partner beside Him) meets disgust; the mention of rivals meets happiness. That pairing is the diagnosis, and anyone can put the question to himself without needing a scholar: *what does my heart do when Allah alone is named, and what does it do when something else is?*

## Ayah 46: the du'ā that answers the disease

Ibn Kathir marks the transition plainly: **after condemning the idolaters for their love of Shirk and their hatred of Tawhid, Allah then says: "Say: O Allah! Creator of the heavens and the earth…"** The cure for a heart that recoils from Allah alone is to *call upon Allah alone*. The verse does not merely argue; it teaches speech.

Ibn Kathir unpacks the opening as: **call upon Allah Alone with no partner or associate, Who has created the heavens and the earth and originated them** — that is, in his phrase, made them "like nothing that ever before existed."

*'Ālim al-ghayb wa'l-shahādah* — **All-Knower of the unseen and the seen** — means, says Ibn Kathir, **what is secret and what is open.**

*"You will judge between Your servants about that wherein they used to differ"* — Ibn Kathir explains that they differed **in this world**, and *"You will judge between them on the Day when they are resurrected and brought forth from their graves."* Every dispute left unsettled here is filed there.

## From the Sunnah: how the Prophet ﷺ began the night

Both commentaries bring the same hadith for this ayah, and both name **Sahīh Muslim**.

Ibn Kathir reports that Abu Salamah bin 'Abdur-Rahman said: "I asked 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, how the Messenger of Allah ﷺ started his prayer when he stood up to pray at night." She said that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up to pray at night, he would start his prayer with these words. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same supplication from Sahīh Muslim, with 'Abd-ur-Rahmān Ibn 'Awf (may Allah be pleased with him) as the one who asked Sayyidah 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) what the Prophet ﷺ began his night prayer (tahajjud) with. The two books give the same supplication; here is Ibn Kathir's rendering of it:

> **O Allah, Lord of Jibrīl, Mīkā'īl and Isrāfīl, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You will judge between Your servants concerning that wherein they differ. Guide me with regard to that wherein there is dispute concerning the truth by Your leave, for You guide whomsoever You will to the straight path.**

Look at what the Prophet ﷺ did with the verse. He took its names — Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, the One who judges between His servants concerning their differences — and made them the doorway into his night prayer, then added the request: **guide me to the truth in what is disputed.** The verse says Allah will settle every dispute on the Day of Resurrection; the du'ā asks to be shown the right side of it now.

**A supplication that is answered.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from al-Qurtubī that Sa'īd Ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) said he knew a verse of the noble Qur'an after reciting which the prayer one makes is answered — and he pointed to this very verse, from *Allāhumma Fāṭir as-samāwāti wa'l-arḍ* to the end of 39:46.

**Etiquette when Muslims disagree.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that someone asked Rabī' Ibn al-Khaitham about the martyrdom of Sayyidnā Husain (may Allah be pleased with him). He sighed, recited this ayah — *"O Allah, Creator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You will judge between Your servants…"* — and said: **whenever you have a doubt in your heart about the mutual differences of the noble Sahābah, do recite this verse.** Tafsīr Rūh ul-Ma'ānī, quoted by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, reports this statement and comments that it teaches us the best etiquette in regard to this issue, and is something one should always bear in mind.

## Ayat 47–48: the Day the accounts open

Now the passage returns to the people of ayah 45 and shows them at the end of the road.

**The ransom that is refused (47).** *"And those who did wrong"* — Ibn Kathir identifies them as **the idolaters**. If they had all that is on the earth and **as much again** with it, they would offer it to ransom themselves from the evil torment — that is, says Ibn Kathir, from what Allah has decreed for them on the Day of Resurrection. **But the ransom will not be accepted from them**, he writes, even if it were to be an earth-full of gold, as Allah mentioned elsewhere (3:91). Wealth has no purchasing power in that reckoning — and doubling it changes nothing.

**The shock (47).** *"And there will become apparent to them from Allah what they had not been reckoning."* Ibn Kathir: **when they come to realise what Allah's punishment for them will be, which they had never before imagined.** The verse's own word is *reckoning* — what waits for them is precisely what their calculations had left out.

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a warning that turns the verse inward. It reports from al-Qurtubī that the famous *tābi'ī* — a member of the generation that came after the Companions — Sufyān Thawrī recited this ayah and said, repeating the sentence twice: **"Ruined are those who did good deeds only to pretend their piety before people. This verse is about them."** They did good deeds in their mortal life to impress people, who took them to be good people. Even they themselves used to deceive themselves by thinking those deeds would become a source of salvation for them in the Hereafter. But as these were never performed with unalloyed sincerity (*ikhlāṣ*), they deserve no reward in the sight of Allah — so once they are in the life after death, the punishment comes upon them suddenly, against their expectation. That is what "what they had not been reckoning" can mean for a person who never bowed to an idol at all.

**The deeds shown, the mockery closing in (48).** *"And the evils of that which they earned will become apparent to them"* — Ibn Kathir: **they will see the punishment for the forbidden actions and sins which they committed in this world.** Then *"and that which they used to mock at will encircle them"*: the punishment which they used to make fun of in this world **will encompass them.** Warnings laughed off are not disposed of; they are only deferred.

## Living it

*The passage's own diagnosis, turned into practice.*

- **Use ayah 45 as a mirror.** Ibn Kathir tells us what the "mention" in this verse is: *there is no true deity except Allah Alone*. Say it deliberately and watch what the heart does — and notice the second reading too: what makes it happy. His warning applies broadly: a heart that will not take in good does not stay empty.
- **Guard against pride, not just idols.** The parallel Ibn Kathir cites (37:35) names the mechanism: they were **too proud to follow it.**
- **Take up the Prophet's ﷺ night-prayer opening.** It is short, it is recorded in Sahīh Muslim, and it is the passage's own remedy — Allah's names, then the plea to be guided to the truth in what people dispute.
- **Recite ayah 46 before you ask.** Sa'īd Ibn Jubayr's practice, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits from al-Qurtubī, was to treat this verse as the one after which a supplication is answered.
- **Refer contested matters — including the differences among the Sahābah — to the Judge.** That is Rabī' Ibn al-Khaitham's counsel, and Rūh ul-Ma'ānī calls it the best etiquette on the question.
- **Audit your intention, not only your deeds.** Sufyān Thawrī's reading of ayah 47 is the most unsettling line in the passage: it is possible to arrive with a full record and find the reckoning was never the one you were keeping.

passages.title: "I was given it by my knowledge"
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat trace a single human pattern from beginning to end: a man in trouble turns to Allah with everything in him, and then, the moment relief arrives, he explains the relief away as something he obtained by his own knowledge. Ayah 49 shows the reflex and the boast; ayah 50 shows that the boast is not new; ayah 51 shows what it cost the people who made it before and warns that it will cost the present ones too; ayah 52 supplies the one piece of knowledge that dissolves the whole illusion. What holds the passage together is a single word played against itself — **knowledge**. He claims to have obtained his blessing "only because of knowledge"; Allah replies that most of them **do not know**; and the passage closes by asking, "**Do they not know** that Allah expands provision for whom He wills and restricts it?"

## The setting: self-deception, continued

Just before this passage, in ayah 47, the Qur'an speaks of a day when "there will appear to them from Allah what they have never imagined." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records, on the authority of Qurtubi, that the famous *tābiʿī* Sufyān Thawrī recited this verse and said — repeating the sentence twice — that ruined are those who did good deeds only to pretend their piety before people. (A *tābiʿī* is a believer of the generation after the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ — those who learned the faith directly from the Companions.) Such people, he said, performed those deeds in this life to impress others, who took them to be good people; they even deceived themselves into thinking that such deeds would become a source of salvation for them in the Hereafter. But because those deeds were never performed with unalloyed sincerity (*ikhlāṣ* — doing an act purely for Allah, with no eye on any audience), they deserve no reward in the sight of Allah, and once they are in the life after death the punishment comes upon them suddenly, against their expectation.

That is the note our passage picks up. Ayah 47 exposes a man deceived about his **deeds**; ayat 49–52 expose a man deceived about his **blessings**. In both cases the self-deception is comfortable, sincere-feeling, and fatal — and in both cases reality arrives from a direction he was not watching.

## Ayah 49: the reflex, and the amnesia

**"When one is touched with hardship, they cry out to Us ˹alone˺."** Ibn Kathir summarises the movement of the whole verse plainly: Allah tells us how man, when he is suffering from harm, prays to Allah, turning to Him in repentance and calling upon Him — but when He makes things easy for him, he transgresses and commits sins.

Notice how little it takes. The verb the Qur'an chooses is *massa* — harm merely **touches** him. It does not crush him or level him; it brushes against him, and immediately the prayer is there, urgent and unforced. This is a compliment to human nature and an indictment of it at the same time. The instinct is sound: under pressure, the created being knows exactly where to turn, and turns there without needing to be taught. The problem is that the instinct is not matched by a memory.

Then comes the turn of the verse: *thumma idhā khawwalnāhu niʿmatan* — "then when We have changed it into a favour from Us," in the rendering Ibn Kathir works with. The hardship is not merely lifted; it is **changed** into a favour. The very situation that had him calling out is turned by Allah into something good. And precisely at that point, at the moment when the traces of divine mercy are most visible, he says: *innamā ūtītuhu ʿalā ʿilm* — "Only because of knowledge I obtained it."

## "Only because of knowledge I obtained it"

Ibn Kathir gives two ways of hearing this claim.

**First — "Allah knows I deserve it."** Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *because Allah knows that I deserve it; if it were not for the fact that Allah regards me as special, He would not have given me this.* This is the more religious-sounding version of the boast, and therefore the more dangerous. The man does not deny Allah. He confesses that Allah gave it — and then quietly makes himself the reason. The gift becomes a certificate. Prosperity becomes proof of merit, and by an easy step, proof of Allah's approval.

**Second — Qatādah's reading.** Ibn Kathir cites Qatādah, who said the meaning is: *"Because I know that I deserve it."* The centre of gravity shifts: in the first reading the knowledge is Allah's knowledge of the man's worth; here it is the man's own knowledge, his own certainty about what he is owed. Either way, the sentence ends where it began — with himself.

Note the word *innamā*, which the rendering carries as **"only."** He is not saying his knowledge was **one** factor among others. He is saying it was **the** factor. Everything else, including the One he was calling upon a moment earlier in the same verse, is edited out of the account.

## "Nay — it is only a trial"

Allah's answer is a single short clause: *bal hiya fitnah*. **"Nay, it is only a trial."**

Ibn Kathir unpacks it: *the matter is not as he claims; on the contrary, We have blessed him with this as a test to see whether he will be obedient or disobedient — although We have prior knowledge of that. In fact, it is a trial.*

Two things deserve to be sat with here.

**One: the blessing itself is the test.** We are used to thinking of hardship as the trial and comfort as the reward for passing it. This verse reverses the picture. The wealth, the recovery, the sudden ease after a hard season — that is the exam paper, not the certificate. *Fitnah* is the Qur'anic word for a testing, a putting-through-the-fire. In Ibn Kathir's words, the blessing arrives with a question attached: will he be obedient or disobedient?

**Two: Allah already knows the answer.** Ibn Kathir is careful to add "although We have prior knowledge of that." Allah does not test in order to find out; His knowledge precedes the event. That the test is nonetheless real, and that a person truly meets his own choices in it, is exactly what Ibn Kathir holds together in one sentence — the blessing *is* a genuine test, *and* Allah's knowledge of its outcome already stands. Neither half cancels the other.

Then: *wa lākinna aktharahum lā yaʿlamūn* — **"but most of them know not."** Ibn Kathir's comment is deliberately deflating: *so they say what they say and claim what they claim.* The man who opened his mouth with "only because of **knowledge** I obtained it" is closed with "most of them do not **know**." The one commodity he was proudest of is the one thing he does not have.

## Ayah 50: "Those before them said it"

**"The same had already been said by those ˹destroyed˺ before them."** Ibn Kathir: *the previous nations who came before said the same things and made the same claims.*

This one sentence takes the boast out of the individual's mouth and puts it into history. He thinks he has arrived at an original insight about his own life. In fact he is reciting lines that have been spoken by nation after nation, and the outcome of the speech is already on record.

*Fa-mā aghnā ʿanhum mā kānū yaksibūn* — **"yet all that they had earned availed them not."** Ibn Kathir: *what they said was not right, and all that they had gathered did not save them.* Two failures in one clause. The **claim** was false; and the **hoard** was useless. Everything they had gathered — the capital, the standing, the security — turned out to have no purchasing power at the only moment when purchasing power mattered.

The word for what they gathered is from *kasb*, "earning" — the very word their pride rested on. They called it earning; Allah calls it earning too, and then shows what earning is worth when the reckoning comes.

## Ayah 51: the same verdict, twice

**"So the evil ˹consequences˺ of their deeds overtook them."** The Arabic keeps *kasb* running: *fa-aṣābahum sayyi'ātu mā kasabū* — the evil results **of what they earned** struck them. What they earned did not save them; what they earned came back and hit them. That is the sharpest turn in the passage. The thing they trusted became the instrument of their ruin.

Then the verse pivots from the past to the present. Of *wa-lladhīna ẓalamū min hā'ulā'i* — "and those who did wrong of these" — Ibn Kathir says simply: **"the people who are addressed here."** The warning steps out of history and into the room where the Qur'an is being heard. And of them Allah says *sa-yuṣībuhum sayyi'ātu mā kasabū*, "they **will** also be overtaken by the evil results of what they earned" — Ibn Kathir adds, *just as happened to those earlier peoples.* The verb carries the future prefix *sa-*: it has not fallen yet. The delay is not an acquittal.

*Wa mā hum bi-muʿjizīn* — **"and they will never be able to escape."** However far a man runs, and however much he has gathered to run with, he cannot put himself beyond Allah's reach.

## The case study: Qārūn

To show that this is not an abstraction, Ibn Kathir points to the one man in the Qur'an who said these exact words. When Qārūn's people told him — *"Do not exult, verily, Allah likes not those who exult. But seek, with that wealth which Allah has bestowed on you, the home of the Hereafter, and forget not your portion of lawful enjoyment in this world; and do good as Allah has been good to you, and seek not mischief in the land. Verily, Allah likes not the corrupters"* — his reply was: **"This has been given to me only because of the knowledge I possess."** And the Qur'an answers him with a question: *Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations, men who were stronger than him in might and greater in the amount of riches they had collected?* (28:76–78)

Look at what his people offered him — a complete, humane programme: enjoy your lawful share, invest in the Hereafter, be good to people as Allah has been good to you, do no corruption. He answered all of it with one sentence about himself. And the refutation is not a sermon; it is a fact of history. Stronger men with bigger fortunes had already been destroyed. The "knowledge" he was so sure of did not even include the previous chapter of the story he was standing in.

Ibn Kathir places alongside it another sentence of the same family: **"And they say: 'We are more in wealth and in children, and we are not going to be punished'"** (34:35). Here the logic is laid bare — abundance is read as immunity. That is the whole error in nine words.

## Ayah 52: the knowledge that undoes the claim

**"Do they not know that Allah expands the provision for whom He wills, and straitens it?"** Ibn Kathir: *He gives plenty to some and restricts the provision for others.*

This is the corrective, and it is aimed exactly at the boast. Provision — *rizq* — moves according to Allah's will. He expands it for whom He wills and restricts it. Once that is grasped, the whole inference collapses: **wealth is not a verdict.** You cannot read a man's standing with Allah off his balance sheet — not another's, and not your own. The rich man's riches do not certify him, and the constrained man's constraint does not condemn him.

Notice, too, how the verse is phrased: not "do they not believe" but **"do they not know."** The claim was made in the name of knowledge; it is dismantled in the name of knowledge. What he called knowledge was a story he told himself. What Allah calls knowledge is seeing who actually opens and closes the hand.

**"Verily, in this are signs for the folk who believe."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief and exact: *there is a lesson and proof.* The same facts lie in front of everyone — some prosper, some struggle, fortunes rise and fall. To one person these are just conditions. To the believer they are **āyāt**, signs: a lesson and a proof. The data is public; the reading requires faith.

## Living it

The passage is intensely practical, and it asks for a few concrete things.

**Watch the moment after the relief.** The danger point in ayah 49 is not the hardship; it is the ease that follows. When the diagnosis comes back clear, when the money lands, when the crisis passes — that is where the verse says a man's tongue changes. Deliberately return the credit at exactly that moment: name it as *niʿmah*, a favour from Allah, out loud, before the explanation of your own competence has time to form.

**Distrust the pious version of the boast.** Ibn Kathir's first reading is the one most likely to catch a religious person: not "there is no Allah," but "Allah gave me this because He knows I deserve it." If you find yourself reading your comfort as a grade on your character, ayah 49 has already answered: *bal hiya fitnah* — it is a trial, and the trial is still running.

**Read your blessings as a question, not a conclusion.** Every increase arrives asking whether you will be obedient or disobedient with it. That is what Qārūn's people urged on him: take your lawful portion, seek the home of the Hereafter with what Allah has given you, do good as Allah has been good to you, and seek no mischief in the land.

**Stop grading people by provision.** Ayah 52 undercuts both directions of the judgement — looking down on the constrained, and looking up to the expanded. Allah expands and straitens as He wills.

**Remember that delay is not safety.** Ayah 51 says the wrongdoers being addressed *will* be overtaken by the evil results of what they earned, just as the earlier peoples were, and that they will never be able to escape. A boast that has not yet been answered is not a boast that has been accepted.

passages.title: Do not despair of Allah's mercy; turn back now
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat are one continuous invitation with a closing door. Ayat 53–55 are Allah's call to every sinner — no matter how far gone — to come back to Him, and to do it *now*; ayat 56–59 show us the moment the offer expires, when the same person stands on the Day of Resurrection and wishes, three times over, that he had taken it. The hinge that holds the passage together is time. Mercy is boundless in its scope, but it is not boundless in its window.

## The people who thought they were beyond forgiveness

The occasion of revelation is what makes this passage land. Ibn Kathir cites Al-Bukhari's report from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): some of the people of *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) had killed many people and committed *zina* (unlawful sexual relations) to a great extent. They came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "What you are saying and calling us to is good; if only you could tell us that there is an expiation for what we have done." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same account through the Tābiʿī (a member of the generation after the Companions) Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, with their words filled out: the religion you invite us to is, no doubt, very good, but we have a problem — we think about all those major sins we have already committed; now if we were to become Muslims, do you hope that our repentance will be accepted?

That is the question this passage answers. These were not Muslims worried about missed prayers. They were people who had killed and who had lived in open sin, standing at the edge of Islam, held back by the weight of their own record. And Allah's answer came down not as a legal ruling but as a *call*: **Say — O My servants.** Ibn Kathir notes the report is also recorded by Muslim, Abu Dawud and An-Nasa'i.

Al-Hasan Al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him) put his finger on what is astonishing here: "Look at this generosity and kindness! They killed His close friends but He still called them to repentance and forgiveness."

## "My servants" — the word choice that carries the whole ayah

Notice who is being addressed in ayah 53. Not "O criminals," not "O idolaters" — **yā 'ibādī**, *O My servants*. Allah still claims them. The relationship is spoken of as intact even while the indictment is being read.

And the indictment is gentle. Ibn Kathir's rendering of **asrafū 'alā anfusihim** is "transgressed against themselves"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "acted recklessly against their own selves." Either way the direction of the harm matters: it is *against themselves*. The damage of sin is described as self-inflicted, not as an injury to Allah. That framing is itself an invitation — a man who has only wounded himself can be treated.

Then the command: **lā taqnaṭū min raḥmat Allāh** — *Despair not of the mercy of Allah.* Ibn Kathir draws out exactly what that forbids: one must not despair of the mercy of Allah **even if his sins are many and great, for the door of repentance and mercy is expansive**. It is that conclusion — *I am finished, there is no way back* — and not the sins themselves, that this ayah comes to demolish.

Ibn Kathir sums up the reach of the ayah: it is a call to all sinners, be they disbelievers or others, and Allah will forgive all the sins of those who repent and turn back to Him, no matter what or how many they are, "even if they are like the foam of the sea."

## The condition that must not be dropped

Ibn Kathir is careful here, and we should be too. He states plainly that this **cannot be interpreted as meaning that sins will be forgiven without repentance**, because *shirk* can only be forgiven for the one who repents from it. He reviews the hadiths on the ayah and concludes: "All of these Hadiths indicate that what is meant is that Allah forgives all sins provided that a person repents."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same line and adds the deadline: well before death arrives, repentance from sins — no matter how serious, even from *kufr* (disbelief) and *shirk* — is accepted; by virtue of a genuine *taubah* (repentance), all sins will be forgiven; therefore no one should lose hope in the mercy of Allah.

So the ayah is not a licence. It is an open door, and a door is only useful to someone who walks through it.

## How wide the door is: Ibn 'Abbas's list

Ali bin Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) a commentary on this ayah worth reading slowly. Allah invites *all* to His forgiveness: those who claim divinity for the Messiah; those who claim the Messiah is the son of Allah; those who claim 'Uzayr is the son of Allah; those who claim Allah is poor; those who claim the Hand of Allah is tied up; those who say Allah is the third of three. To all of these Allah says, *Will they not turn in repentance to Allah and ask His forgiveness? For Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful* (5:74).

*(A note of my own, not from the two tafsirs: what Ibn 'Abbas lists here are false sayings about Allah. The believer's own path is to affirm of Allah what He has affirmed of Himself, as the early generations did — without likening Him to creation and without emptying His words of meaning.)*

Then Ibn 'Abbas goes one step further: Allah calls to repentance even the one who said something worse than all of that — the one who said, *I am your Lord most high*, and *"I know not that you have a god other than me"* (28:38). Even a man who claimed lordship over people was still being called back.

Ibn 'Abbas then drew the conclusion that gives this ayah its edge: **"Anyone who makes the servants of Allah despair of His mercy after this, has rejected the Book of Allah"** — adding, "but a person cannot repent until Allah decrees that he should repent." Both halves belong together. It is a sin against the Book to tell a sinner he is finished; and it is Allah's decree, not our own cleverness, that turns a heart back in the first place.

Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) is reported by At-Tabarani, through Shutayr bin Shakal, as saying that the ayah in the Qur'an **which brings the most relief** is this one in Surat Az-Zumar — and Masruq said to him, "You have spoken the truth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar likewise said this verse carries the strongest message of hope for sinners, while Ibn 'Abbas held that the strongest such verse is *And surely, your Lord is the lord of forgiveness for the people against their wrongdoings* (Ar-Ra'd 13:6). The scholars differed on which ayah is most hope-giving; they did not differ that hope is the point.

## From the Sunnah

Under the heading "Hadiths which tell us not to despair," Ibn Kathir gathers narrations for exactly this ayah:

- **Asma' bint Yazid** (recorded by Imam Ahmad, also by Abu Dawud and At-Tirmidhi) said she heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite this ayah with an addition after "Allah forgives all sins" — rendered in Ibn Kathir's text as *"He does not reckon him."*
- **Anas bin Malik** (recorded only by Ahmad): "By the One in Whose Hand is my soul, if you were to commit sin until your sins filled the space between heaven and earth, then you were to ask Allah for forgiveness, He would forgive you. By the One in Whose Hand is the soul of Muhammad, if you did not commit sin, Allah would bring other people who would commit sins and then ask Allah for forgiveness so that He could forgive them."
- **Abu Ayyub Al-Ansari**, on his deathbed, said he had concealed something he heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "If you did not commit sins, Allah would create people who would sin so that He could forgive them." Recorded by Imam Ahmad, also by Muslim in his *Sahih*, and by At-Tirmidhi.
- **The man who killed a hundred** — the hadith of Abu Sa'id recorded in the Two Sahihs. He had killed ninety-nine, then asked a worshipper among the Children of Israel whether he could repent; the man told him no, so he killed him too, completing a hundred. Then he asked one of their scholars, who said: "What is stopping you from repenting?" and told him to go to a town where Allah was worshipped. He set out, and death came to him on the road. The angels of mercy and the angels of punishment disputed over him, so Allah commanded them to measure the distance between the two towns; whichever he was closer to would claim him. They found he was closer to the town he was heading for, so the angels of mercy took him. It was said that as he was dying he moved himself towards that town, and Allah commanded the good town to move closer to him and the other to move away.

Read that last one against Ibn 'Abbas's warning. The worshipper who said "no" is the cautionary figure of this passage; the scholar who said "what is stopping you?" is the one who understood the ayah.

## Ayat 54–55: what repentance actually looks like

Having opened the door, Allah says how to walk through it, and the verbs are all of movement.

**Ayah 54: *anībū ilā rabbikum wa aslimū lahu*.** Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: turn back to Allah and submit yourselves to Him. Repentance is not merely regret — it is a turning back and a handing over. And it has a cut-off: *before the torment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, hasten to repent and do righteous deeds before His wrath comes upon you. Once it arrives, no help is available from any quarter.

**Ayah 55: *wattabi'ū aḥsana mā unzila ilaykum min rabbikum*** — follow the best of what has been sent down to you. Ibn Kathir says plainly: this means the Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Qurtubi, opens it out: the whole Qur'an is *aḥsan* — the best — and it can also be called the best and most perfect in the sense that out of all the scriptures revealed by Allah, the Torah, the Injīl and the Zabūr, the Qur'an is the best and the most complete.

So the sequence is: stop despairing (53), turn back and submit (54), then live by the Book (55). Repentance is not a feeling you have once; it is entry into a life shaped by revelation.

And ayah 55 tightens the clock further than ayah 54 did: *before the torment comes on you* **suddenly** *while you perceive not* — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, without you realizing it. Ayah 54 warns that punishment will come; ayah 55 warns that you will get no notice. That is the strongest argument in the passage for repenting today rather than at some sensible later date.

## Ayat 56–58: the three regrets

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads these three ayat as an elaboration and reinforcement of 53–55: no sinner of any description should despair of the mercy of Allah, for should he repent, Allah will forgive all his past sins — but the opening phrase **an taqūla nafsun** ("lest someone should say") reminds us that the time of *taubah* (repentance) has a deadline, and it has to be well before death. Remorse produced after death, on the Day of Judgement, brings no benefit at all. These three ayat are the negative image of the first three: this is what it looks like when the invitation is left unanswered.

**Regret one (ayah 56): "Alas, my grief that I was undutiful to Allah — and I was indeed among those who mocked."** Ibn Kathir: on the Day of Resurrection the sinner who neglected to repent and turn back to Allah will regret it, and will wish he had been one of the righteous who obeyed Allah. And the confession *"I was indeed among those who mocked"* means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "my actions in this world were those of one who ridicules and makes fun, not of one who has firm faith and is sincere." A person can spend a life mocking without ever intending to — simply by living as though none of it were serious.

**Regret two (ayah 57): "If only Allah had guided me, I should indeed have been among those who have taqwā"** — that is, among those who fear Allah and guard themselves against His displeasure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes this sharply: even in a place like that there will be the odd person who would love to wriggle out of the impasse by blaming his destiny — had Allah given me the necessary guidance I too would have been one of those who feared Him, but since He gave me no guidance, there was nothing I could do about it.

**Regret three (ayah 58): "If only I had another chance, then I should indeed be among the doers of good."** Ibn Kathir: he will wish he could go back to this world so that he could do righteous deeds.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a fine observation on sequence. These three wishes may belong to three different people — or they may have come one after the other from a single group. The clue is in ayah 58, which says the third is spoken *when he sees the torment*, which suggests the first two belong to a time before the punishment is seen. So: on the very first day of Qiyamah they remember the shortcomings of their deeds and cry out in grief (56); then, as an excuse, they plead that they were helpless and unguided (57); and finally, once they see the punishment, they wish to be sent back into the world (58). Grief, then excuse, then bargaining — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, that will be a time when no wish and no remorse of any kind will work.

Ibn 'Abbas, in the report of Ali bin Abi Talhah, notes something quietly overwhelming about these ayat: **Allah tells us what His servants will say before they say it, and what they will do before they do it** — citing *And none can inform you like Him Who is the All-Knower* (35:14). The excuses of the Last Day have already been published, in advance, so that we can hear how they sound while there is still time not to make them.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Each of the people of Hell will be shown his place in Paradise and he will say, 'If only Allah had guided me!' so it will be a source of regret for him. And each of the people of Paradise will be shown his place in Hell and he will say, 'If it were not for the fact that Allah guided me,' so it will be a cause of thanks." It was also narrated by An-Nasa'i. The same fact — that guidance is from Allah — becomes anguish in one mouth and gratitude in the other.

## Ayah 59: the answer

The passage closes with Allah's reply, and it begins with a single sharp word: **balā** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "Yes!" and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "Why not?" *Yes! Verily, there came to you My Ayat and you denied them, and were proud and were among the disbelievers.*

Ibn Kathir paraphrases: 'O you who regret what you did, My Ayat did come to you in the world, and My proof was established against you, but you rejected it and were too arrogant to follow it, and you were among those who disbelieved in it.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 59 as the direct answer to the excuse of ayah 57: Allah had already given the necessary guidance, fully and conclusively — He had sent His books, verses and signs — so their claim that Allah gave them no guidance was absurd. What Allah did not do, once the guidance had been given, was *force* anyone to be good and obedient. Every servant of His was given the choice to take either the way of truth or the way of falsehood; that was the test, and on it depended success or failure. Whoever took to the way of error by his own free will, choice and volition is himself responsible for it.

Note the three failures ayah 59 names in order: **denial** (*fa-kadhdhabta*, "you called them untrue"), **pride** (*wastakbarta*, "you waxed proud"), and finally settled **disbelief**. The middle one is the pivot. Pride is what turned an available truth into a rejected one — the same arrogance in Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: they were "too arrogant to follow it."

## Living it

Read as one unit, this passage asks three concrete things.

**Refuse despair — and refuse to inflict it.** Whatever your record, the ayah addresses you as *My servant*, and Ibn 'Abbas's verdict stands over anyone who tells a sinner otherwise. If you are the friend, the parent, the imam someone comes to with a terrible confession, the model is the scholar in the hadith, not the worshipper: *what is stopping you from repenting?*

**Refuse presumption.** Ibn Kathir will not let the ayah be read as forgiveness without repentance. The door is open; you still have to move.

**Move now.** Ayah 54 says before the punishment comes; ayah 55 says it may come suddenly, without you realizing it; ayat 56–58 replay, in advance, exactly what you will say if you wait. Repentance postponed to a moment of your choosing assumes you will be given that moment. Nothing in this passage grants that assumption.

And ayah 55 tells you what the turning is *for*: not a moment of remorse but a life reoriented around the best of what was sent down. Turn back, submit yourself to Him, and then follow the Book.

passages.title: Faces darkened, the mindful delivered
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close a long passage of warning with a single scene held in two halves: on one side, the people who lied about Allah, their faces blackened, with Hell named as the abode fit for the arrogant; on the other side, those who had taqwā, delivered by Allah Himself. What holds ayah 60 and ayah 61 together is that contrast — the same Day, the same crowd, two utterly different outcomes — and the quality that divides them: **arrogance** on one side, **taqwā** on the other.

*Taqwā* is the Qur'an's word for being mindful of Allah — careful of Him in what you do. Our translation of ayah 61 renders it simply: "those who were mindful of Him."

## What has just been said

To feel the force of these two ayat you have to hear what precedes them. Maarif ul Quran points back to ayah 57, where the disbelievers said: *"If Allah were to show me the way, I would have surely been among those who fear Allah."* It is the oldest excuse there is — *nobody told me; I was never guided.* Ayah 59 answers it in Allah's own voice: *"Why not? My verses had reached you, but you called them untrue, and waxed proud, and became of those who disbelieved."*

Maarif ul Quran draws out what that answer establishes. Allah had already given the necessary guidance, fully and conclusively: He had sent His books, His verses and His signs. So their claim that Allah gave them no guidance was absurd. But — and this is the crucial second half — once He had given the guidance, Allah never forced anyone to be good and obedient. Every servant of His was given the choice: the way of the truth or the way of the false. That choice *was* a test for the one making it, and on it depended his or her success or failure. Whoever took to the way of error by his own free will, choice and volition is himself responsible for it.

That is the argument our two ayat now settle in visible form. Ayah 60 is not a new topic; it is the verdict on a case already argued. The excuse has been examined and answered, and now we are shown what the excuse-maker looks like when the verdict lands.

## "You will see those who lied about Allah"

The address is direct — *tarā*, "you will see." The scene is not reported from a distance; the listener is placed there as a witness.

And notice how the guilty are named. Not "those who sinned," not "those who were weak," but **those who lied about Allah** — those who spoke about Him what was not true. Ibn Kathir specifies what the lie was: their claims **that He had partners or offspring**. That is the lie of this passage. To say Allah has a partner, or a son, or a daughter, is not a private opinion about theology; it is false testimony given about the Lord of the worlds. Everything else in the ayah follows from it.

**Their faces will be black** (*wujūhuhum muswaddah*). Ibn Kathir's comment is short and exact: their faces are black **because of their lies and fabrications**. The punishment is not arbitrary; it is the outward form of what they did. They spoke falsely about Allah, and on the Day when everything hidden is made visible, the falsehood shows on them. In this life a lie can be dressed up, argued for, inherited as respectable tradition. On that Day it wears its own face.

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on these two ayat with a wider statement. Allah tells us that on the Day of Resurrection, **some faces will be blackened and some will be whitened**: the faces of those who followed splits and divisions will be blackened, and the faces of *Ahlus-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah* will be whitened. We affirm what is reported here — faces genuinely darkened, faces genuinely brightened — as Allah has said it, without inventing a mechanism for it and without emptying it of its meaning.

## "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?"

The second half of ayah 60 is a question, and questions like this in the Qur'an are rarely requests for information. *Alaysa fī jahannama mathwan lil-mutakabbirīn* — "Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?" Ibn Kathir unfolds it as: **is not Hell sufficient for them as a prison and humiliating final destination, because of their stubborn pride, arrogance and refusal to follow the truth?** The question is really an answer. It invites the listener to look at the crime and agree that the sentence fits.

Two words carry the weight.

**Mathwā** — rendered "abode," and Ibn Kathir's gloss sharpens it to a prison and a humiliating final destination. Not a stop on a journey: the place where the journey ends, and where the one who arrives is held and brought low.

**Al-mutakabbirīn** — "the arrogant." See how precisely this answers ayah 59, which said of these same people that they *"waxed proud."* Their problem was never a shortage of evidence; the verses had reached them. Ibn Kathir names the cause as **stubborn pride, arrogance and refusal to follow the truth** — not inability, refusal. So the humiliation of Hell is the exact reversal of the posture they chose: those who would not lower themselves are lodged in a humiliating final destination.

Notice too that ayah 60 has moved from *lying about Allah* to *arrogance*. That is the diagnosis. The false claim about Allah was the symptom; the swollen self was the disease.

## The turn: "And Allah will deliver those who were mindful of Him"

Ayah 61 turns the whole scene over, and the first thing to notice is who acts. *Wa yunajjī-llāhu* — **and Allah will deliver.** Not "they will escape," not "they will be found innocent." The subject of the verb is Allah. On a Day whose greater terror this same ayah will mention in a moment, those who had taqwā are not left to save themselves; they are delivered.

**Those who had taqwā** — *alladhīna-ttaqaw*. Set them against the previous ayah and the contrast is complete. The arrogant refused to follow the truth and are given a humiliating final destination; those who were mindful of Allah are delivered to their places of success. And recall the excuse quoted in ayah 57 — *"I would have surely been among those who fear Allah."* Ayah 61 shows the speaker the people who actually were.

**Bi-mafāzatihim** — "to their places of success." Ibn Kathir explains that Allah delivers them **because of what Allah has decreed for them of happiness and victory** — their deliverance is not a lucky escape but the arrival of something already decreed for them. Where the arrogant have a *mathwā*, an abode in Hell, those with taqwā have a *mafāza*, a place of success. Two destinations, set side by side so you can see the whole map at once.

## "Evil shall touch them not, nor shall they grieve"

The ayah then guarantees their safety twice — from the outside, then from the inside.

**"Evil shall touch them not"** (*lā yamassuhumu-s-sūʾ*). Ibn Kathir specifies the timing: **on the Day of Resurrection**. On the Day when evil is everywhere, none of it reaches them.

**"Nor shall they grieve"** (*wa lā hum yaḥzanūn*). This is the inward half, and Ibn Kathir's comment on it is the warmest line in the passage: **the greater terror of that Day will not cause them grief, for they will be safe from all grief and removed from all evil, and they will attain all that is good.** Read those three clauses slowly, because they are three separate gifts. *Safe from all grief* — nothing left inside to ache. *Removed from all evil* — the harm is not merely survived, it is put at a distance. *They will attain all that is good* — the account does not end at rescue; it ends at receiving. All around them the Day is at its most terrifying, and it does not get in.

## Living it

**Be careful what you say about Allah.** The people ruined in ayah 60 are ruined by speech about their Lord that was not true — by lies and fabrications, as Ibn Kathir puts it. That should make a believer cautious in a very practical way: about declaring something permitted or forbidden without knowledge, about "Allah surely wants…" said off the top of the head, about passing on religious claims we have not verified. Speaking about Allah is testimony, and testimony can be false.

**Watch for pride, not only for doubt.** Ayah 59 and ayah 60 together say that this ruin was not an information problem. The verses had reached them. What stopped them was that they *waxed proud*, and Ibn Kathir names it as stubborn pride and refusal to follow the truth. The honest question to put to yourself is not only "do I know?" but "when the truth turned out to be inconvenient, did I follow it?"

**Own your choice.** Maarif ul Quran's point is a heavy mercy: Allah gave the guidance fully and conclusively, then never forced anyone — every servant was given the choice, and that choice was the test. That removes every alibi — and it also means nothing has been decided against you behind your back.

**Let ayah 61 be the picture you hold.** The believer's hope in these ayat is not placed in his own strength. It rests on a verb whose subject is Allah: *He* delivers. Taqwā is what you bring; the deliverance is what He does. And what waits at the other end is not bare survival but a place of success, where no evil touches you and nothing is left to grieve over.

passages.title: The keys are His: worship none but Him
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the surah's long argument by moving from who Allah is to what that means you must do. Ayat 62–63 establish His total ownership of everything that exists; ayat 64–66 draw the only conclusion that ownership allows — worship Him alone, and be thankful.

## The thread that holds the passage together

The logic runs in one straight line. **He created everything** (62). **To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth** (63). Therefore **directing worship anywhere else is refused outright**, even when the refusal is put in the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ himself (64–65). So: **worship Him, and be grateful** (66).

Notice the word *losers* (*al-khāsirūn*) stitching the passage together. In ayah 63 those who disbelieve in the āyāt of Allah "are the losers." In ayah 65 the same word returns in the warning about associating partners with Allah: "you will certainly be among the losers." The passage names loss in terms of belief and worship, not of wealth or worldly defeat.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the wider frame from a few ayat earlier. Ayah 59 answers what the disbelievers had said in ayah 57 — that had Allah shown them the way, they would have been among those who fear Him. The answer is that Allah had already given the necessary guidance, fully and conclusively: He sent His books, His verses and His signs, so the claim that He gave them no guidance was baseless. And yet, having given guidance, Allah never forced anyone to be good and obedient. Every servant was given the choice to take either the way of truth or the way of falsehood; this was a test for the one making the choice, and on it depended his or her success or failure. Whoever took the way of error by his own free will bears the responsibility himself. Our passage is what that choice actually comes down to: Him, or something else.

## Ayah 62: Creator, and Trustee over all things

*"Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the Maintainer."*

Two claims, and the second is the one people quietly forget. Many will concede that Allah made the world. Fewer live as though He is still running it. The Arabic word here is *wakīl*, rendered in our sources as "Maintainer" and as "Trustee over all things."

Ibn Kathir unpacks the pair of statements together: Allah tells us here that He is "the Creator, Lord, Sovereign and Controller of all things; everything is subject to His dominion, power and guardianship."

Four words, and no gap left between them. Creation is not a past event Allah has stepped back from. The same One who brought things into being is named in that same breath as their Lord, their Sovereign and their Controller — and everything, without remainder, falls under His dominion, His power and His guardianship.

That is the premise. Everything after it is consequence.

## Ayah 63: "To Him belong the keys"

*"To Him belong the maqālīd of the heavens and the earth."*

This is the image the whole passage is named for, and it repays a close look.

**The word itself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *maqālīd* is the plural of *miqlād* or *miqlīd*, meaning a key. It notes that the word has been said to be Arabicized from Persian: in Persian a key is *kalīd*; brought into Arabic it became *iqlīd*, whose plural is *maqālīd* (the commentary here is drawing on *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*). Ibn Kathir records the same point from the earliest generations: **Mujahid** said, "Maqalid means 'keys' in Persian," and this was also the view of **Qatadah**, **Ibn Zayd** and **Sufyan bin ʿUyaynah**.

**A second reading.** **As-Suddi** understood the phrase to mean "the treasures of the heavens and the earth" — not the keys but what the keys open. Ibn Kathir does not treat this as a rival meaning to be defeated. He observes that both opinions arrive at the same place: "the control of all things is in the Hand of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, for His is the dominion and to Him is the praise, and He is able to do all things."

(A note on wording: the source speaks of things being "in the Hand of Allah." As Ahl al-Sunnah, we affirm what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ affirmed of the divine attributes, as the early generations did — without likening them to anything in creation, and without emptying them of meaning.)

**Why the image is so exact.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what the metaphor is doing: "Having keys in one's hand denotes ownership, possession and the ability to dispense at will." A key is not merely access. The one holding the key is the one who decides whether the door opens, for whom, and how far. So, it concludes, the sense of the ayah is that the keys to whatever treasures lie hidden in the heavens and the earth are in the hands of Allah, "and He alone is the custodian and the dispenser in that it is He who gives whenever He wills to whomever He wills and as much as He wills — and would just not give to anyone He so wills."

Sit with what that rules out. Whatever treasures lie hidden in the heavens and the earth lie behind doors, and there is exactly one custodian and one dispenser. Nobody else has a spare set of keys. This is why the ayah's second half is not a change of subject: **"And those who disbelieve in the āyāt of Allah — such are they who will be the losers."** Ibn Kathir glosses *āyāt* here as "His proof and evidence." To reject the proof and the evidence, on this description of who Allah is, is what the ayah calls loss.

## Ayat 64–65: the question put to the Prophet ﷺ

*"Say: 'Do you order me to worship other than Allah, O you fools!'"*

**What prompted this.** Ibn Kathir reports the reason for the revelation, narrated by **Ibn Abi Hatim and others from Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him): the idolaters, in their ignorance, called the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to worship their gods, and then they would worship his Lord with him. It was offered as an exchange — a settlement in which each side keeps something.

Then these words were revealed.

**Why "fools."** The Arabic is *al-jāhilūn* — those characterised by *jahl*, ignorance. Ibn Kathir's report of the occasion uses exactly that register: the idolaters called him "in their ignorance." The word is not an insult thrown in temper; it names the condition the proposal comes out of. Set the offer next to ayat 62–63 — Allah the Creator of all things, the keys of the heavens and the earth His alone — and you can see what the ayah is calling ignorant.

There is also something to learn in the form of the reply. The Prophet ﷺ is told *qul* — "say." He is not given a negotiating position. He is given words, and the words are a question put back to the ones who made the offer.

**Ayah 65: the stakes.** *"And indeed it has been revealed to you, as it was to those before you: 'If you join others in worship with Allah, surely your deeds will be in vain, and you will certainly be among the losers.'"*

Two things are worth noticing.

First, this is not a new rule announced for the Arabian situation. It was revealed "to you, and to those before you" — the same terms were given to the prophets who came before. This is the unchanging clause in revelation.

Second, look who is being addressed. The warning is put to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself. Ibn Kathir places the ayah beside the verse of Sūrat al-Anʿām: **"But if they had joined in worship others with Allah, all that they used to do would have been of no benefit to them"** (6:88).

The heading Ibn Kathir gives this whole passage says it plainly: associating others in worship with Allah *cancels out* good deeds. That is the passage's answer to the everyday assumption that sincerity of any kind is enough, that all roads climb the same mountain. On this teaching, the direction of worship is not a detail of the journey; it is the journey.

## Ayah 66: the command, and the closing word

*"Rather, worship Allah alone, and be one of the grateful."*

The Arabic opens with *bal* — rendered "Nay! But," "Rather." The offer of ayah 64 is not answered with a counter-offer. It is set aside, and a command is put in its place.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah and widens the address: the meaning, he says, is that "you and those who follow you and believe in you should make your worship sincerely for Allah Alone, with no partner or associate."

So the command is not the Prophet's ﷺ alone. It lands on everyone who claims to follow him — and Ibn Kathir's word for what is required is *sincerely*: worship for Allah alone, with nothing set beside Him.

**And why gratitude?** Because it is the fitting response to ayat 62–63, and the passage would be unfinished without it. If everything that exists is the creation of Allah, and the keys to the treasures of the heavens and the earth are in His hands alone, then *shukr* — thankfulness — is simply an accurate reaction to reality. Worship without gratitude is duty performed at arm's length; gratitude without worship is a feeling that never becomes an act. The ayah asks for both, and asks you to *be among the grateful* — not to perform an occasional act of thanks, but to belong to that company.

## A note on a narration about this ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions that in some narrations of hadith, the third kalimah — *subḥān Allāh, wal-ḥamdu lillāh, wa lā ilāha illa'llāh, wa'llāhu akbar, wa lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh al-ʿaliyy al-ʿaẓīm* ("Pure is Allah and Praised is Allah and there is no god worthy of worship but Allah and Allah is Great and there is no strength and there is no power except from Allah, the High, the Great") — has been called "the keys to the heavens and the earth," the outcome being that whoever recites this kalimah mornings and evenings is blessed by Allah from the treasures of the heavens and the earth.

The commentary is careful about the status of these reports, and we should be too: **Ibn al-Jawzi declared these narrations fabricated (*mawḍūʿ*)**, while **other hadith experts rated them weak (*ḍaʿīf*)** — the kind, the commentary notes, that can be relied upon in the matter of the merits of good deeds. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this discussion to *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*.) No collection is named in our source, and so we name none either. The words themselves are remembrance of Allah; it is the specific promise attached to them that the scholars disputed.

## Living it

**Check what you are actually asking of creation.** The keys are held by One, who is the sole custodian and dispenser, giving when He wills, to whom He wills, and as much as He wills. When you find yourself convinced that a person, an institution, or a stroke of luck is what will open the door, ayah 63 is asking you to look again at whose hands the keys are in.

**Refuse the exchange.** The offer in ayah 64 rarely arrives today wearing idols. It arrives as the suggestion that a little accommodation in what you hold sacred is the reasonable, neighbourly thing. The answer given to the Prophet ﷺ was not a better deal. It was *bal* — nay; rather.

**Guard the direction of your worship as carefully as its quantity.** Ayah 65 says that joining others in worship with Allah leaves deeds in vain. Sincerity for Allah alone — Ibn Kathir's own word for what this ayah asks — is not one virtue among many.

**Let thankfulness be the shape of it.** Ayah 66 does not end with "worship." It ends with belonging to the grateful. The One who holds the keys gives whenever He wills, to whomever He wills — and you are living on what He has already given.

passages.title: They did not esteem Allah as He deserves
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat begin with a charge — that the idolaters never took the true measure of Allah — and then answer that charge with a scene: the Day when everything they refused to weigh correctly becomes visible, audible and inescapable. Ayah 67 states the failure; ayat 68–70 show what it looks like when the reality finally arrives, with the whole earth in His grasp and the heavens rolled up in His Right Hand, the Trumpet sounding, the earth lit up for judgement, and every soul paid in full. The accusation and the scene are one argument: they underestimated Him, and here is what they underestimated.

## "They made not a just estimate of Allah"

Ibn Kathir explains the opening words simply: **the idolaters did not give Allah His due when they worshipped others alongside Him.** He is the Almighty and there is none mightier; He is the One able to do all things; He is the Owner of all things, and everything is under His control and power. To set anything beside such a Being is not merely a ritual error — it is a failure of measurement.

The early authorities cited by Ibn Kathir approach the phrase from slightly different angles, and together they map out what "not measuring Allah properly" means:

- **Mujahid** said, "This was revealed concerning Quraysh."
- **As-Suddi** said, "They did not venerate Him as He deserves to be venerated" — a failure of reverence.
- **Muhammad bin Ka'b** said, "If they had made a just estimate of Allah such as is due to Him, they would not have lied" — a failure that shows up in the tongue. A person who truly grasps who Allah is cannot lie comfortably.
- **Ibn 'Abbas** (may Allah be pleased with him), through the report of 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, gave the sharpest formulation: "These are the disbelievers who did not believe that Allah had power over them. **Whoever believes that Allah is able to do all things, has made a just estimate of Allah such as is due to Him, and whoever does not believe that, has not made a just estimate of Allah such as is due to Him.**"

Notice how those readings differ in emphasis — the translations in front of you reflect the same range, one rendering the phrase as failing to make a *just estimate*, another as failing to show *proper reverence*. Estimating and revering are two faces of one act: you honour what you have correctly sized up. Ibn 'Abbas's version is the most testable one. It turns the ayah from an accusation aimed at a people long gone into a question aimed at you: do you actually believe Allah has power over you — over your income, your health, your plans, the outcome you are quietly certain of? Wherever the answer wobbles, that is exactly where the ayah is speaking.

## The rabbi, and the Prophet's ﷺ smile

Ibn Kathir notes that **many hadiths have been narrated concerning this ayah**, and that it and other ayat like it are to be interpreted and accepted "without any attempts to twist or change the meaning."

**Al-Bukhari recorded** that 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: one of the rabbis came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Muhammad! We learn that Allah will put the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the trees on one finger, the water and dust on one finger, and the rest of creation on one finger, then He will say: *I am the King.*" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ **smiled so broadly that his molars could be seen**, in confirmation of what the rabbi had said, and then recited this very ayah. Ibn Kathir notes that Al-Bukhari recorded it in other places of his Sahih as well, and that it was also recorded by Imam Ahmad and Muslim, and by At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i in the books of Tafsir in their Sunans.

Sit with that smile for a moment. A man from outside the community brings a description of Allah's majesty, and the Prophet ﷺ does not merely nod — his face opens with delight, and the ayah comes to his lips as the Qur'an's own confirmation. This is the response of someone who *has* measured Allah rightly: joy at His greatness, not discomfort at it.

Three further narrations in Ibn Kathir fill out the same scene:

- **Abu Hurayrah** (may Allah be pleased with him) heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "Allah will grasp the earth and roll up the heavens in His Right Hand, then He will say: *I am the King, where are the kings of the earth?*" Ibn Kathir notes this version was recorded only by Al-Bukhari, with Muslim recording another version.
- **Ibn 'Umar** (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "On the Day of Resurrection, Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, will grasp the earth with one finger, and the heavens will be in His Right Hand, then He will say, *I am the King.*" Recorded by Al-Bukhari.
- Ibn 'Umar also said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this ayah one day on the minbar — the raised pulpit from which he addressed the people — and said, moving his hand forward and backward: "And the Lord will glorify Himself, saying *I am Compeller, I am the Proud, I am the King, I am the Mighty, I am the Most Generous.*" **And the minbar shook so much that we feared the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would fall.** Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Muslim, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

"Where are the kings of the earth?" is the question the whole passage is built around. Every power that ever made a person afraid, every authority that seemed too large to name — on that Day there is simply no one to answer.

## How the scholars hold these words

Ayah 67 speaks of the whole earth being in *a single grip* of His hand (qabḍah — a grasp, a grip, a handful) and the heavens *rolled up* on His Right Hand. How is that to be understood?

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reports two positions, and keeps them carefully apart.

**The early forbears of Islam** took the earth being in the hand-grip of Allah and the heavens being rolled up on His right hand **in its real sense** — that is, they affirmed exactly what Allah said of Himself, without reinterpreting it. At the same time, the subject of the verse falls into the category of **al-mutashābihāt** (verses of hidden meaning), whose reality is known to no one but Allah; for people in general even trying to find out that reality is forbidden. What is left to do is to believe that whatever Allah means by it is true and correct.

And because the apparent words suggest a grasp, a grip, a hand holding something, and a right hand — things that in our experience are parts of a body, while Allah is pure and free from body and physicality — **the end of the ayah itself releases a hint**: *Glorified be He, and High be He above all that they associate as partners with Him.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that closing clause as saying: **do not take these words on the analogy of your own body limbs.** Allah is free from these.

**Later day scholars**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān continues, took the verse to be metaphorical, explaining that having something grasped in the hand and having something in the right hand is an allusion to **having something under full possession and control** — and that this perfect possession and control is what is meant here. That is a different move from the first position: it reads the wording as an image standing for something else rather than affirming it in its real sense.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān does not settle between the two. It closes the discussion with the words of a scholar who knows where the limit is: *And Allah, He is pure and high — He knows best.* And whichever position one holds, two guardrails from the sources remain in place: Ibn Kathir's counsel that such ayat are accepted without any attempt to twist or change their meaning, and the ayah's own final clause declaring Allah far above anything creation could be likened to Him.

## Ayah 68: the Trumpet, and the silence after it

Ibn Kathir says Allah here tells us of **the terrors of the Day of Judgement, with its mighty signs and terrifying upheaval.**

The blast named in ayah 68 is, in Ibn Kathir's reckoning, **the second trumpet-blast — the one that causes people to die.** Everyone alive in the heavens and on the earth is caused to die by it, *except him whom Allah wills*. Then the souls of the remaining creatures are taken, **until the last one to die is the Angel of Death**, and there remains only the Ever Living, Eternal One, who was there in the beginning and will be at the end, forever. Three times He will say, *"Whose is the kingdom this day?"* — and then answer Himself: *"It is Allah's, the One, the Irresistible!"* (40:16). Ibn Kathir glosses that answer: *I am the One existing Alone, I subjugated all things and I decreed that all things must come to an end.*

**On the word ṣaʿiqa.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word used — *ṣaʿiqa* — literally means to swoon, faint or fall unconscious. The sense is that all will first become unconscious and then die; and those who had already died, their spirits too will become unconscious. (The same commentary points out that the parallel passage in Sūrah an-Naml uses *faziʿa*, "frightened", instead.) The word is chosen for what it does to the imagination: not a tidy announcement of an ending but a shock that flattens everything standing.

**"Except him whom Allah wills."** Who is spared? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from the narrations of *ad-Durr al-Manthūr*, that four angels are included — **Jibrāʼīl, Mīkāʼīl, Isrāfīl and ʿIzrāʼīl** (the angel of death) — and, as in some narrations, the angels bearing the Throne as well. Their exemption means only that the blowing of the sūr does not cause death to them; **later on, they too will meet their death**, and no one but the one and single Being of Allah will remain alive at that time. Ibn Kathir, the commentary notes, opted for this view, and said that even out of all of them the angel of death will be the last to die.

Then: *Then it will be blown another time, and behold they will be standing, looking on.* Ibn Kathir calls this **the third trumpet-blast, the trumpet-blast of Resurrection.** Isrāfīl is the first to be brought back to life, and Allah commands him to sound the Trumpet again. After being bones and dust, people come alive, looking at the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir sets it beside *"But it will be only a single Zajrah, when behold, they find themselves alive"* (79:13–14), and *"Then afterwards when He will call you by a single call, behold, you will come out from the earth"* (30:25). Note the speed built into all of these: no process, no interval — a sound, and then everyone is on their feet.

**Al-Bukhari recorded** from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Between the two blasts, there will be only forty." People asked him: forty days? forty years? forty months? To each, Abu Hurayrah answered, "I do not know." That honest refusal to fill a gap is itself a lesson in how knowledge is handled. In the same narration: "Every part of a man will disintegrate apart from the root of his backbone, and out of that he will be created anew."

Ibn Kathir also cites a long narration from 'Abdullah bin 'Amr (may Allah be pleased with him), which he attributes to Imam Ahmad and notes was recorded by Muslim in his Sahih, describing the sequence of end-times events: the Dajjal emerging in the Ummah and staying among them for "forty" — the narrator unsure whether he said days, months, years or nights; then Allah sending ʿĪsā bin Maryam (peace be upon him), who resembles ʿUrwah bin Masʿūd ath-Thaqafī and who prevails, and Allah destroys the Dajjal; then seven years in which there is no enmity between any two people; then a cool wind from the direction of ash-Shām that takes the soul of every person with even a speck of faith in his heart — even one who was inside the heart of a mountain. What remains is "the most evil of people, as light as birds and with the hard hearts of wild predators," who recognise no good and denounce no evil, and who worship idols at Shayṭān's prompting — **while their provision is ample and their standard of living good.** Then the Trumpet is blown, and no one hears it without tilting his head to listen. **The first one to hear it is a man who is filling his water trough**, and he dies when he hears it.

That detail is the whole point in miniature. The Hour does not wait for a dramatic moment. It comes upon a man in the middle of an ordinary chore, among people who were doing well.

## Ayah 69: light, the record, and the witnesses

*And the earth will shine with the light of its Lord.* Ibn Kathir explains: it will shine brightly on the Day of Resurrection **when the Truth — Allah, may He be glorified and exalted — manifests Himself to His creation, to pass judgement.** The court does not need lamps; the light comes from the Judge.

*And the Book will be presented.* **Qatādah** said: "The Book of deeds."

*And the Prophets will be brought forward.* **Ibn 'Abbas** (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "They will bear witness against the nations, testifying that they conveyed the Message of Allah to them." No nation will be able to plead that it was never told.

*And the witnesses.* Ibn Kathir understands these as **witnesses from among the angels who record the deeds of all, good and evil alike.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the circle, showing from the Qur'an itself who will stand as witness on the plains of Resurrection:

- **the prophets** — *"We shall bring a witness from every community"* (4:41);
- **the angels** — *"with each someone to drive and someone to bear witness"* (50:21), where the driver and the witness are established as angels (citing *Tafsīr ad-Durr al-Manthūr*);
- **the followers of the Prophet of Islam ﷺ** — *"and so that you become witnesses to other people"* (22:78);
- **and one's own body limbs** — *"their hands will speak to Us and their feet will bear witness"* (36:65).

Read that list slowly. The testimony comes from above you, beside you, and from your own body. There is no angle left from which a case can be denied.

*And it will be judged between them with truth* — Ibn Kathir: **with justice** — *and they will not be wronged.* He supports this with *"And We shall set up Balances of justice on the Day of Resurrection, then none will be dealt with unjustly in anything. And if there be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it. And Sufficient are We to take account"* (21:47), and *"Surely, Allah wrongs not even the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good done, He doubles it, and gives from Him a great reward"* (4:40). Note the asymmetry in that second ayah: strict justice on the debit side, multiplication on the credit side.

## Ayah 70: paid in full

*And each person will be paid in full of what he did* — Ibn Kathir: **of good and evil.** Nothing is skimmed, nothing is lost, nothing is inflated. *And He is Best Aware of what they do.*

That closing clause quietly seals the passage. The books, the prophets, the angels, the testifying limbs — none of it exists because Allah needs evidence. He is already Best Aware of what was done. The record is presented for *you*, so that the verdict lands on a soul that can no longer argue with it.

## Living it

The passage begins with an accusation about measurement and ends with an accounting. That is not a coincidence — it is the argument.

- **Test your estimate of Allah where it actually operates.** By Ibn 'Abbas's standard, believing Allah is able to do all things *is* measuring Him rightly. The place to check is not your creed statement but your anxiety: what you fear, who you think can really harm or help you, whose approval reorganises your day.
- **Let His greatness make you glad, not tense.** The Prophet ﷺ smiled until his molars showed when Allah's majesty was described. Awe and delight belong together.
- **Live as though the man at the water trough is you.** The Trumpet finds people mid-task, comfortable, well provided for. Ordinary competence at ordinary work is no protection.
- **Speak truthfully.** Muhammad bin Ka'b's remark deserves repeating: had they measured Allah properly, they would not have lied. Honesty is theology showing up in the mouth.
- **Take comfort in the exactness.** *They will not be wronged* is not only a warning. Every unseen good you did, every injustice done to you that no one recorded — a mustard seed's weight of it is brought forward. Deeds done where no one was watching were always being watched.

passages.title: The two throngs driven to Hell and Paradise
passages.tafsir:
These are the closing ayat of Sūrat az-Zumar: humanity moving in two great processions, one driven to Hell, one led to Paradise, and the gates of each opening to receive them. What holds ayat 71–75 together is a deliberate mirroring: the same opening words, the same arrival, the same gatekeepers speaking — and then everything diverges.

## The scene just before

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out ayah 69, "and the prophets and the witnesses will be brought": at the time of reckoning on the plains of Resurrection, present there will be all the prophets and all the other witnesses. The prophets are themselves among the witnesses — "We shall bring a witness from every community" (4:41). Angels are among them — "with each someone to drive and someone to bear witness" (50:21), where Maʿārif notes, citing Tafsīr Ad-Durr-ul-Manthūr, that the driver and the witness have been clearly established as being angels. The followers of the Prophet ﷺ are witnesses too — "so that you become witnesses to other people" (22:78). And a person's own limbs will testify — "their hands will speak to Us and their feet will bear witness" (36:65).

## "Driven" — the verb that opens both processions

Ayah 71 begins **wa-sīqa** — "and they were driven." Ayah 73 begins with the identical verb: **wa-sīqa alladhīna ttaqaw rabbahum**. Same passive verb, and the same word for the crowds — **zumaran**, which Ibn Kathir renders "in groups."

For the first throng, Ibn Kathir spells out what the driving means: Allah tells us "how the doomed disbeliever will be driven to Hell by force, with threats and warnings." He gathers the parallels. "The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing" (52:13). "The Day We shall gather those who have taqwā unto the Most Gracious, like a delegation. And We shall drive the criminals to Hell, in a thirsty state" (19:85–86). And in that state, Ibn Kathir adds, "they will be blind, dumb and deaf, and some of them will be walking on their faces" (17:97).

For the second throng, Ibn Kathir describes an entirely different movement: believers taken to Paradise "in groups, one group after another, starting with the best of them: those who are closest to Allah, then the most righteous, then the next best and the next best." And "each group will be with others like them, Prophets with Prophets, the true believers with their peers, the martyrs with their counterparts, the scholars with their colleagues, every group composed of people of the same kind."

## Two arrivals, two openings

**The first gate (ayah 71).** "Till when they reach it, the gates thereof will be opened." Ibn Kathir: "as soon as they arrive, the gates will be opened quickly, in order to hasten on their punishment."

Then the keepers speak — "stern angels, severe and strong," says Ibn Kathir, speaking "by way of rebuking and reprimanding":

- *"Did not the Messengers come to you from yourselves?"* — Ibn Kathir: "of your own kind, so that you could have spoken to them and learned from them."
- *"reciting to you the āyāt of your Lord"* — "establishing proof against you that what they brought to you was true."
- *"and warning you of the meeting of this Day of yours"* — "warning you of the evil of this Day."

The answer is a single word: **balā** — "Yes." Ibn Kathir: "they did come to us and warn us and establish proof and evidence against us." Then, "but the Word of torment has been justified against the disbelievers," which he glosses as their own admission: "but we rejected them and went against them… because we had turned away from the truth towards falsehood."

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it: a keeper asks "Did no warner come to you?" and they answer, "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied him and said: 'Allah never revealed anything; you are only in great error'" — and then, "Had we but listened or used our intelligence, we would not have been among the dwellers of the blazing Fire!" (67:8). Ibn Kathir: "they will feel regret and will blame themselves." And of the ayah that follows — "Then they will confess their sin. So, away with the dwellers of the blazing Fire!" (67:11) — he says: "they are lost and doomed."
