**"It will be said" — a sentence with no speaker.** Ayah 72 opens **qīla**, a passive verb: *it was said*. Ibn Kathir: "everyone who sees them and the situation they are in, will testify that they deserve the punishment. These words are not attributed to any specific person, but they are said as an indication that the entire universe will bear witness that they deserve what they are suffering, in accordance with the judgement of the Most Just, the All-Knowing."

"Enter the gates of Hell, to abide therein" means "to stay there forever; you will never leave or depart." And the closing verdict names the disease: *"what an evil abode of the arrogant"* — **al-mutakabbirīn**. Ibn Kathir: "what an evil destiny and what an evil place to stay, because of your arrogance in this world and your refusal to follow the truth; this is what has led you to this."

## The second arrival — and the sentence Allah does not finish

Ibn Kathir explains that "till when they reach it" means "when they arrive at the gates of Paradise, after passing over the Sirāt, where they will be detained on a bridge between Paradise and Hell, and any injustices that existed between them in this world will be settled until they have all been purified from sin through this trial. Then permission will be granted for them to enter Paradise."

In ayah 71 the words are *futiḥat abwābuhā* — "its gates were opened." In ayah 73 there is an extra letter: *wa-futiḥat abwābuhā*. Ibn Kathir reads the result as a sentence deliberately left hanging: "This is a conditional sentence that is not complete." What it implies, he says, is that "when they come to the gates of Paradise the gates will be opened for them as a sign of honor, and the angelic gatekeepers will meet them with glad tidings, greetings of peace and praise. Unlike the gatekeepers of Hell who will meet the disbelievers with rebuke and reprimand, the believers will be filled with happiness and joy, each according to his degree of luxury and delights." And then: "What happens after this is not mentioned; it is left for the imagination to think of its dearest wishes and be filled with hope."

Hell's sentence is closed and final. Paradise's is left open.

## At the gates

Ibn Kathir notes what is known from the ṣaḥīḥ ḥadīths — Paradise has eight gates.

**Who opens them.** It was recorded in the ḥadīth about the Trumpet that when the believers reach the gates of Paradise they will consult one another as to who should ask permission for them to enter. They will ask Adam, then Nūḥ, then Ibrāhīm, then Mūsā, then ʿĪsā, then Muhammad — may blessings and peace be upon them all — akin to what will happen in the arena of judgement. Ibn Kathir says this is "to show the noble position of Muhammad ﷺ above the rest of mankind in all situations." In **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**, from Anas, he ﷺ said, "I will be the first intercessor in Paradise," and, in Muslim's wording, "I will be the first one to knock at the gates of Paradise." **Imam Ahmad** recorded from Anas bin Malik — and it was also recorded by **Muslim** — that he ﷺ said: "I will come to the gate of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection and will ask for it to be opened. The gatekeeper will say, 'Who are you?' I will say, 'Muhammad.' He will say, 'I was told about you and that I was not to open the gate for anyone before you.'"

**Who enters first.** **Imam Ahmad** recorded from Abu Hurayrah — and it was also recorded by **al-Bukhari and Muslim** — that the first group to enter Paradise will enter "looking like the moon on the night when it is full." They will not spit there, or blow their noses, or defecate; their vessels and combs will be of gold and silver, their censers of aloeswood, their sweat musk; "there will be no disputes between them and there will be no hatred; their hearts will be as if one heart. They will glorify Allah morning and evening." **Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abu Yaʿlā** recorded a similar report — which **al-Bukhari and Muslim** also produced from the ḥadīth of Jābir — adding that those who follow that first group will look "like the brightest star shining in the sky."

**The seventy thousand.** From Abu Hurayrah, recorded by **al-Bukhari and Muslim**: "A group of my Ummah, seventy thousand, will enter Paradise with their faces shining like the moon on the night when it is full." Ukkāshah bin Miḥṣan stood up and said, "O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah to make me one of them." He said, "O Allah, make him one of them." Then one of the Anṣār stood and asked the same, and he ﷺ said, "Ukkāshah has beaten you to it." Ibn Kathir notes that this ḥadīth — about the seventy thousand who will enter Paradise without being brought to account — was also recorded by **al-Bukhari and Muslim** from Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir bin ʿAbdullāh, ʿImrān bin Ḥuṣayn, Ibn Masʿūd, Rifāʿah bin ʿArābah al-Juhanī and Umm Qays bint Miḥṣan, and from Abu Hazim from Sahl bin Saʿd: "Seventy thousand or seven hundred thousand of my Ummah will surely enter Paradise, holding on to one another, such that the first and last of them will enter Paradise together."

**Which gate is yours.** **Imam Ahmad** recorded from Abu Hurayrah — with something similar recorded by **al-Bukhari and Muslim** — that whoever spends a pair of something from his wealth for the sake of Allah will be called from the gates of Paradise: "Whoever is among the people of prayer, will be called from the gate of Prayer; whoever is among the people of charity, will be called from the gate of Charity; whoever is among the people of Jihād, will be called from the gate of Jihād; whoever is among the people of fasting, will be called from the Gate of ar-Rayyān." Abu Bakr asked whether anyone would be called from all of them, and he ﷺ said, "Yes, and I hope that you will be one of them." And in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim**, from ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb, whoever performs wuḍūʾ and does it well and then says, "I testify that there is none worthy of worship except Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger" — "the eight gates of Paradise will be opened for him and he will enter through whichever one he wishes."

**How wide.** On the width of those gates, Ibn Kathir pauses to pray: "We ask Allah to make us among its people." Then, in the **Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, from Abu Hurayrah in the lengthy ḥadīth about intercession: Allah will say, "O Muhammad, admit those of your Ummah who are not to be brought to account, through the right-hand gate, and they will be counted among those who will enter from other gates as well" — and "the distance between the two gateposts of the gates of Paradise is like the distance between Makkah and Hajar." According to another report: between Makkah and Buṣrā. And it was recorded in **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim** from ʿUtbah bin Ghazwān that he ﷺ told them the distance between the two gateposts of Paradise was the distance of a forty-year journey, "but there would come a day when they would be packed with crowds of people."

## "Peace be upon you — you have done well"

The greeting in ayah 73 is **salāmun ʿalaykum ṭibtum** — "Salām ʿalaykum (peace be upon you)! You have done well." Ibn Kathir renders the meaning: "your deeds and words were good, and your efforts were good, and your reward is good." The first word a believer hears at that gate is *salām* — the greeting he has been giving and returning all his life.

Ibn Kathir adds that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ issued commands during some of his military campaigns that it should be shouted out to the Muslims: "No one enters Paradise except a Muslim soul" — or, according to one report, "a believing soul." And *"enter here to abide therein forever"* means "to dwell therein, never seeking any change."

## What the people of Paradise say (ayah 74)

Their first speech is not a request. It is praise. Ibn Kathir: "when the believers see the great reward and splendors, blessing and grand generosity, they will say, *al-ḥamdu lillāh alladhī ṣadaqanā waʿdah*" — Allah "has fulfilled His promise to us," meaning "the promise which He made to us through His Messengers who called us to this in the world." Ibn Kathir sets alongside it their duʿāʾ from this life — "Our Lord! Grant us what You promised unto us through Your Messengers and disgrace us not on the Day of Resurrection, for You never break Your promise" (3:194) — and their words in 7:43: "All the praises and thanks be to Allah, Who has guided us to this, and never could we have found guidance, were it not that Allah had guided us!" — and in 35:34–35: "All the praises and thanks be to Allah Who has removed from us all grief… Who, out of His grace, has lodged us in a home that will last forever, where toil will touch us not nor weariness will touch us."

**"And made us inherit the land."** Abu al-ʿĀliyah, Abu Ṣāliḥ, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Ibn Zayd all said this means the land of Paradise; Ibn Kathir links it to "My righteous servants shall inherit the land" (21:105).

**"We can dwell in Paradise where we will."** Ibn Kathir: "wherever we want, we can settle; how excellent a reward for our efforts." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication: apart from their own special dwelling places, the people of Jannah "will be allowed to visit others there and take pleasure trips around."

And here Maʿārif tells a story that turns geography into longing. Ṭabarānī, Abu Nuʿaym and Ḍiyāʾ have reported, through a chain rated *ḥasan*, from Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah, that someone came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I love you so much that I keep thinking of you even when I go back home, and I remain uncomfortable and impatient until I return to you. But when I remember my death and remember your death, it occurs to me that you will be in the higher stations of Jannah, and even if I reach there somehow, it is certain that I shall be on a level much below it. My worry is: how am I going to see you?" The Prophet ﷺ remained silent — until Jibrāʾīl came with the verse: "And those who obey Allah and the Messenger are with those whom Allah has blessed, namely, the prophets, the Ṣiddīqīn, the Shuhadāʾ and the righteous — and what a good company they are" (4:69). (Maʿārif explains: *Ṣiddīq* means "very truthful," referring to those Companions of a prophet who excel all others in submission to Allah and His Messenger, like Sayyidnā Abu Bakr; *Shuhadāʾ*, the plural of *shahīd*, means those who sacrificed their lives in the way of Allah.) Maʿārif joins them: our ayah tells us that they will be allowed to visit the higher stations of Jannah. "May Allah Taʿālā, in His mercy, make us join up with them in Jannah."

Ibn Kathir closes with what the Prophet ﷺ himself saw, reported in the **Two Ṣaḥīḥs** from Anas bin Malik in the story of the Miʿrāj: "I was admitted into Paradise where I saw that its domes were pearls and its soil was musk."

## The last ayah: the angels around the Throne

Ayah 75 lifts the camera: "And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne from all round, glorifying the praises of their Lord."

Ibn Kathir explains the angels' *tasbīḥ* here. Allah "tells us how He will pass judgement on the people of Paradise and Hell, and put each of them in the place fitting for him and for which he is suited; this is justice from Him and He is never unjust. Then He tells us of His angels who surround His majestic Throne, glorifying the praises of their Lord, extolling and magnifying Him, and declaring Him to be above any shortcomings or injustice whatsoever, for He has passed judgement in the fairest and most just manner." Their *tasbīḥ* is not decoration; it is the verdict on the verdict. And "they will be judged" means, says Ibn Kathir, all of creation — nobody stands outside that court.

Then the sūrah ends as ayah 72 did — a passive verb, no named speaker: **wa-qīla l-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn**. Ibn Kathir: "all of creation, whether animate or inanimate, will speak words of praise to Allah, the Lord of all that exists, for His wisdom and justice. These words are not attributed to any specific speaker, which indicates that the whole of creation will testify to His praise."

Qatādah saw the shape of it: "Allah began His creation with praise, as He said, *All praises and thanks be to Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth* (6:1) — and He ended it with praise," with this very ayah.

## Living with these ayat

- **Everyone in ayah 71 already knew.** *Balā* — "Yes." Nobody at that gate claims the message never reached them. The tragedy is not ignorance but hearing and turning away.
- **Arrogance is the named cause.** Ayah 72 calls Hell the abode not of the sinful but of the arrogant — "your arrogance in this world and your refusal to follow the truth."
- **You travel in the group you belong to.** Prophets with prophets, the truthful with their peers. Choose now the company you want to be sorted with.
- **Settle your scores here.** Injustices between believers are settled on the bridge before Paradise.
- **Pick your gate — and want them all.** Prayer, charity, jihād, fasting; and for one who performs wuḍūʾ well and says the shahādah, all eight.
- **Their first sentence in Paradise is ḥamd.** Learn the language now: praise for a promise kept.
